This study presents a comprehensive analysis of the generalization error for two-layer neural networks used to solve high-dimensional Schrödinger eigenvalue problems. We demonstrate that the generalization error converges at a rate of $O(N^{-1/2})$, where $N$ represents the number of training samples. Furthermore, we establish that the approximation error can be bounded by $O(N^{-1/2})$ under the condition that the target function is sufficiently smooth. Finally, we prove that the total error converges at a rate of $O(N^{-1/4})$. These findings are derived from a combination of deterministic and probabilistic arguments. Additionally, numerical experiments are conducted to validate the theoretical results. The source code for this work is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2020/Neural-Network-for-Solving-High-Dimensional-Schrodinger-Eigenvalue-Problem. This study introduces a time series regression model designed to forecast the activity of neurons within the C. Elegans nervous system. The proposed method employs a recurrent neural network (RNN) to learn the temporal dynamics of neuronal activity, utilizing a training set where each sample consists of a sequence of activities from all neurons in the organism. The model is trained to predict the activity of a specific target neuron based on the sequence of all neurons. Experimental results demonstrate that the model achieves high prediction accuracy, with a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.99. Furthermore, the model successfully captures the temporal dynamics of the target neuron, as evidenced by a low mean squared error of 0.001. Finally, the model's ability to generalize to unseen neurons is validated by its performance on test data. These findings indicate that the proposed approach is effective for predicting neuronal activity in C. Elegans. This paper aims to identify all strong Gelfand pairs involving the special linear group SL(2,p), where p is a prime number. We demonstrate that for p greater than 3, the only strong Gelfand pair is (SL(2,p), S), with S representing the subgroup of upper triangular matrices. In contrast, when p equals 3, we find that (SL(2,3), S) is not a strong Gelfand pair. Additionally, we provide a complete classification of all strong Gelfand pairs for SL(2,3). As a consequence, we establish that the number of strong Gelfand pairs for SL(2,p) is exactly 1 if p > 3 and 4 if p = 3. Finally, we present a general formula for the character table of SL(2,p). This work extends the findings of [1], which focused exclusively on the case p = 3. Furthermore, we generalize the results of [2] to the scenario where p > 3. The paper concludes with a discussion of the character table for SL(2,3).

This study investigates the electromagnetic characteristics of hidden-charm molecular pentaquarks containing a single strange quark. Utilizing the one-boson-exchange model, we calculate their magnetic moments and radii. Our findings indicate that these properties are highly sensitive to the internal quark configuration. Furthermore, we observe that the magnetic moments of these pentaquarks are significantly smaller than those of their antiparticles. Finally, we compare our results with existing experimental data and other theoretical predictions. The electromagnetic properties of these pentaquarks offer a valuable means to explore their internal structures. Additionally, our calculated magnetic moments align well with experimental measurements, while our predicted radii fall within the range of other theoretical estimates. These outcomes suggest that the molecular pentaquark model remains viable. Finally, we propose that future experiments should focus on measuring the electromagnetic properties of hidden-charm molecular pentaquarks with single strangeness. Such measurements would provide crucial insights into their internal structures and help distinguish between competing theoretical models. This paper investigates the scattering theory for the three-dimensional inhomogeneous nonlinear Schrödinger equation featuring a cubic nonlinearity and an inverse square potential. We demonstrate that the Cauchy problem associated with this equation is locally well-posed within the Sobolev space $H^s(\mathbb{R}^3)$ for $s \geq 1/2$. Furthermore, we establish global well-posedness and scattering in $H^s(\mathbb{R}^3)$ for initial data satisfying $\|u_0\|_{H^s(\mathbb{R}^3)} \leq \epsilon$, where $\epsilon > 0$ is a sufficiently small constant. Additionally, we prove that the scattering theory remains valid for initial data with arbitrarily large norms. Finally, we derive the asymptotic behavior of the solution. These findings extend previous results by removing the smallness assumption on the initial data norm and by eliminating the requirement for the nonlinearity to be subcritical. The methodology employed relies on the Strichartz estimates for the Schrödinger equation with an inverse square potential, the local smoothing effect, and the interaction Morawetz estimate. The primary challenge addressed is the critical nature of the nonlinearity, which is overcome by utilizing the inhomogeneous structure of the equation. Specifically, we apply the fractional chain rule to derive the necessary Strichartz estimates. Finally, we utilize the local smoothing effect and the interaction Morawetz estimate to demonstrate global well-posedness and scattering. The local smoothing effect is derived from the Strichartz estimates, while the interaction Morawetz estimate is obtained through a combination of Strichartz estimates, the fractional chain rule, and the virial identity. This approach yields a global-in-time estimate for the $L^2$-norm of the solution. Consequently, we can prove that the solution remains bounded in $H^s(\mathbb{R}^3)$ for all time, thereby establishing global well-posedness and scattering. We introduce a novel class of migration-contagion processes, which function as a hybrid between migration and contagion mechanisms. In this framework, a population is distributed across multiple sites, where individuals at each location can either move to other sites or be infected by neighbors. We establish a sufficient condition for the extinction of the process and demonstrate that, under specific circumstances, the system converges to a non-trivial stationary distribution. Furthermore, we derive a sufficient condition ensuring the existence of a non-trivial quasi-stationary distribution. Finally, we apply these findings to a specific instance of the migration-contagion process. (This research was partially supported by the National Science Foundation under grant DMS-1106973.) Keywords: Migration-contagion process; Extinction; Stationary distribution; Quasi-stationary distribution. We confirm the existence of a 3:2 mean motion resonance chain within the K2-138 system, which was previously suggested by the Kepler mission. This system comprises a 0.33 M$_\odot$ star hosting four planets with masses ranging from 1.8 to 10.5 M$_\oplus$. Our analysis of the radial velocity data reveals that the planets are locked in a 3:2 resonance chain, with the innermost planet exhibiting a 2:1 resonance with its neighbor. Additionally, we identify a 1:2:4 Laplace resonance among the three innermost planets. We also examine the system's dynamical stability and discuss the implications of these findings for planet formation theories. Finally, we present the updated orbital parameters for the K2-138 system. This research was conducted using the HARPS spectrograph at the ESO 3.6m telescope. Amorphous ice is a subject of intense scientific inquiry, with significant implications for both fundamental physics and practical applications. This study examines the structural characteristics of amorphous ice generated through the vapor deposition of water molecules onto a cold substrate. Utilizing molecular dynamics simulations, we analyze the radial distribution function and the bond angle distribution of oxygen atoms. Our findings indicate that the amorphous ice produced in this manner exhibits a structure comparable to that of crystalline ice. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the amorphous ice can be modeled as a collection of ice domains, each possessing a structure similar to crystalline ice. These results suggest that amorphous ice is not a single, uniform phase but rather a composite of multiple ice domains. Consequently, our approach offers a novel perspective for investigating the structural properties of amorphous ice. Additionally, we show that the amorphous ice generated via vapor deposition on a cold substrate is more ordered than that formed through other methods, such as compression. This suggests that vapor deposition on a cold substrate is a promising technique for creating highly ordered amorphous ice. Finally, we discuss the potential applications of this method in the fields of quantum computing and quantum information processing. Our research provides a new pathway for exploring the structural properties of amorphous ice and for developing novel materials with unique characteristics. Ultimately, this work holds significant potential for advancing our understanding of the fundamental properties of matter and for driving technological progress. This study presents a detailed investigation into the local density of states (LDOS) of graphite, gold, and silicon surfaces using Scanning Tunnelling Microscopy (STM). By employing the constant current mode, we achieved atomic-resolution imaging of the surface topography. Furthermore, utilizing the constant height mode, we mapped the LDOS of these materials. The findings indicate that the measured LDOS aligns with established theoretical models and prior experimental data. Additionally, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of the STM's performance, including its sensitivity, resolution, and stability. Finally, we demonstrated the STM's capability to detect minute surface defects and contaminants on the samples. These results confirm that STM is a highly effective tool for investigating surface properties at the atomic scale. Ultra-low frequency (ULF) waves are a primary focus of magnetospheric research, yet their inaudibility to the human ear has historically hindered their accessibility. This study introduces a method to render these waves audible by applying a frequency shift that preserves their temporal characteristics. We demonstrate this approach using data from the THEMIS spacecraft, which recorded a ULF wave event. The resulting audio reveals the wave's temporal structure, including its onset, duration, and decay. Furthermore, we show that the wave's frequency can be determined by counting the beats per second in the audio. This technique is broadly applicable to ULF wave data, offering a valuable tool for education and outreach. Additionally, we provide a Python script to facilitate the creation of such audio files. This paper introduces a small-step operational semantics for the programming language GP 2, which is a variant of the language presented in "A Language for Generalized Polymorphism" by J. G. R. Doumen and J. Fokkinga (POPL 1995). GP 2 extends the simply typed lambda calculus with a polymorphic type constructor and a corresponding abstraction and application mechanism. The proposed semantics is both sound and complete with respect to the denotational semantics of GP 2. Furthermore, it is proven that GP 2 enjoys strong normalization and subject reduction. Finally, the paper demonstrates that GP 2 is Turing complete by providing an embedding of the untyped lambda calculus into GP 2. The authors intend to utilize this semantics to develop a type-directed compiler for GP 2. Additionally, they plan to investigate the relationship between GP 2 and other polymorphic lambda calculi, such as System F and the calculus of constructions. Photoevaporation and magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) disk wind models offer potential explanations for the observed gas outflows in protoplanetary disks. This study investigates the feasibility of distinguishing between these two mechanisms using future high-angular resolution radio observations of TW Hydrae. We modeled the radio emission from a photoevaporative wind, assuming a temperature of 1000 K and a density of $10^5$ cm$^{-3}$ at 100 au, and compared it against a model of a MHD disk wind. Our results indicate that the photoevaporative wind model produces a radio flux of approximately 10 mJy at 1.3 mm, with a brightness temperature of roughly 1000 K at 100 au. In contrast, the MHD disk wind model yields a significantly lower radio flux of about 1 mJy at 1.3 mm, with a brightness temperature of approximately 100 K at 100 au. We conclude that the photoevaporative wind model is more consistent with the observed radio flux of TW Hydrae. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the photoevaporative wind model can be distinguished from the MHD disk wind model through future high-angular resolution radio observations. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for the study of protoplanetary disk winds. (Abridged)

This paper presents a factoring algorithm for specific variants of Chebyshev polynomials, utilizing the minimal polynomials of $\cos(\frac{2\pi}{d})$ as the basis. The study examines the factorization of $T_n(x)-1$, $T_n(x)+1$, and $T_n(x)-\alpha$, where $\alpha$ is a root of $M_d(x)$. Leveraging the algebraic properties of $M_d(x)$, we derive factorization formulas for these Chebyshev variants. Furthermore, we establish a relationship between the irreducible factors of $T_n(x)-\alpha$ and $M_d(x)$, which facilitates the factorization of $T_n(x)-\alpha$ when $n$ is a multiple of $d$. Finally, we provide an example demonstrating the application of this method. The results are applicable to the factorization of Chebyshev polynomials over the rational numbers $\mathbb{Q}$ and finite fields $\mathbb{F}_p$. Additionally, we offer an alternative proof for the factorization of $T_n(x)-1$ and $T_n(x)+1$ over $\mathbb{Q}$, as presented in [1]. This approach also yields a straightforward formula for determining the degree of the irreducible factors of $T_n(x)-1$ and $T_n(x)+1$ over $\mathbb{Q}$. Finally, we present an example illustrating the factorization of $T_n(x)-\alpha$ over $\mathbb{F}_p$ using this method.

Nuclear masses are essential for modeling the $r$-process, which generates the majority of heavy elements in the universe. However, the extreme conditions of $r$-process environments involve nuclei far from stability, making experimental mass measurements impossible. Consequently, theoretical predictions are necessary, yet current models lack the precision required for $r$-process studies. This study introduces a machine learning approach to predict nuclear masses with the accuracy needed for such applications. We trained a neural network using a dataset of 2,500 masses derived from both experimental data and theoretical models. The resulting network achieves a root-mean-square deviation of 10 keV for experimental masses and 150 keV for theoretical ones. This performance surpasses existing models and meets the accuracy threshold for $r$-process research. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the neural network can be integrated into $r$-process simulations, yielding results consistent with those from other mass models. Finally, we show that the network can be extended to predict masses for nuclei beyond its training set. These findings indicate that machine learning is a viable method for predicting nuclear masses with the precision demanded by $r$-process studies. Sapphire is a widely used dielectric material in quantum technologies, particularly for superconducting qubits and microwave resonators. However, its dielectric loss, which limits the coherence of these devices, remains difficult to measure precisely. We introduce a novel method for inducing anomalous optical drag on atoms, where the force acts in the direction of atomic motion rather than opposing it. This phenomenon is achieved by applying a laser beam that is red-detuned relative to the atomic transition. The resulting anomalous drag force is proportional to the square of the atomic velocity and can be precisely controlled by adjusting the laser's detuning. We demonstrate that this effect can be observed in a magneto-optical trap (MOT) using a single retro-reflected laser beam. Furthermore, we show that this anomalous drag force can be utilized to cool atoms to temperatures below the standard Doppler limit. Finally, we outline potential applications of this optical drag force in the context of atom interferometry. These findings were experimentally validated using rubidium atoms. The anomalous optical drag force is expected to be applicable to other atomic species as well. Additionally, we propose that this effect could be extended to other systems, including molecules, Bose-Einstein condensates, and solid-state systems. This study addresses two-stage robust optimization problems where binary uncertainty parameters are constrained by a cardinality limit. We introduce a Lagrangian dual approach to derive a computationally efficient reformulation of the original problem. This reformulation is solved using a branch-and-cut algorithm that integrates cutting planes derived from the Lagrangian dual. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing approaches in terms of solution time. Furthermore, we apply this reformulation to a two-stage robust unit commitment problem, showing that it yields a more accurate solution compared to the method proposed by Bertsimas et al. (2013). Finally, we illustrate the method's effectiveness through a numerical case study involving a real-world power system. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/robin-berthet/Two-stage-robust-optimization.

Keywords: two-stage robust optimization, binary uncertainty, cardinality constraint, Lagrangian dual, unit commitment.

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have recently gained significant attention for their ability to learn from graph-structured data. However, training GNNs from scratch is often computationally expensive and prone to overfitting, especially when data is limited. Transfer learning offers a solution by enabling the reuse of knowledge gained from one task to improve performance on another. This study investigates transfer learning within the GNN framework, specifically examining how to leverage a source task to enhance a target task. We evaluate various strategies for transferring both model parameters and graph structures, analyzing their impact on performance. Our findings indicate that transfer learning can substantially boost GNN performance, particularly when the source and target tasks share similar graph structures. This represents the first algorithm to achieve both sublinear communication and polylogarithmic rounds. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our method can be adapted to the data stream model, enabling two parties to solve Set Disjointness using $O(n)$ space. This result improves upon the prior best-known space complexity of $O(n \log n)$ established by Indyk and Kushilevitz. Additionally, we show that our algorithm can be extended to the $k$-Set Disjointness problem, where $k$ parties each possess a subset of $[n]$, achieving a communication complexity of $O(k \log n)$. We investigate the nonlinear Hall conductivity in a two-dimensional system featuring broken inversion symmetry, utilizing the Kubo formula. Our analysis demonstrates that the nonlinear Hall conductivity remains robust against disorder and interactions, provided the Fermi level resides within a mobility gap. Furthermore, we establish that the linear Hall conductivity is likewise unaffected by these factors under the same conditions. Finally, we examine the impact of interactions on the Fermi surface and the resulting nonlinear Hall conductivity when the Fermi level is situated within a metallic phase. In this metallic regime, interactions induce a finite density of states at the Fermi level, which subsequently generates a finite nonlinear Hall conductivity. These findings are validated through numerical calculations. Additionally, we explore the potential for observing the nonlinear Hall effect in a two-dimensional topological insulator. Finally, we discuss the experimental feasibility of detecting this phenomenon in the two-dimensional material WTe$_2$. Our results indicate that the nonlinear Hall conductivity in WTe$_2$ is approximately $10^{-10}$ S, a value that is experimentally accessible. This suggests that the nonlinear Hall effect could serve as a valuable tool for characterizing the electronic properties of two-dimensional materials. Finally, we address the relationship between the nonlinear Hall effect and the anomalous Hall effect. We demonstrate that the nonlinear Hall effect can be interpreted as a manifestation of the anomalous velocity, which arises from the Berry curvature dipole. This effect is distinct from the anomalous Hall effect, which is driven by the Berry curvature dipole moment. Consequently, the nonlinear Hall effect can be viewed as a nonlinear response to an electric field, whereas the anomalous Hall effect represents a nonlinear response to a magnetic field. We conclude that the nonlinear Hall effect is a unique phenomenon that can be observed in both insulators and metals. In insulators, it is governed by the Berry curvature dipole, while in metals, it is determined by the Berry curvature dipole moment. This effect is expected to be observable in a wide range of materials, including two-dimensional topological insulators, Chern insulators, and Dirac materials. Our findings provide a theoretical foundation for the experimental detection of the nonlinear Hall effect in two-dimensional materials. We anticipate that this effect will play a crucial role in the development of new electronic devices and technologies. This study examines the thickness-dependent electronic properties of molybdenum and tungsten dichalcogenides (MX$_2$, where X = S, Se, Te) using density functional theory (DFT) and GW methods. We calculated the work function ($\Phi$), ionization energy ($I$), and electron affinity ($A$) for these materials. Our results indicate that $\Phi$ and $I$ decrease as the number of layers decreases, whereas $A$ increases. Specifically, the GW method yields a more accurate work function for monolayer MoS$_2$ compared to DFT, with a value of 4.6 eV. Furthermore, we observe that the band gap of monolayer MoS$_2$ is 2.5 eV within the GW framework, contrasting with the 1.8 eV value obtained from DFT. Finally, we demonstrate that the GW method effectively corrects the underestimation of the band gap in bulk MoS$_2$ caused by DFT. These findings are essential for understanding the electronic characteristics of transition metal dichalcogenides. Delta lenses serve as a formal framework for modeling change management in software systems, specifically addressing how modifications in one system are propagated to another. This paper introduces a novel application of delta lenses to supervised learning, demonstrating that the process can be modeled as change propagation. We establish a formal connection between the two frameworks and outline the resulting benefits. Finally, we discuss the implications of this approach for both software engineering and machine learning. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/robinwittig/dlsl.

This result extends the work of Sogge and Zelditch, who previously addressed the $C^3$ case. As an application, we derive uniform $L^p$ bounds for the spectral projection operators of the Laplace-Beltrami operator on compact manifolds with boundaries. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the remainder term in the Weyl law for the spectral projection operators on compact manifolds without boundary is $o(N^{n/2})$ whenever the metric is piecewise $C^2$. Finally, we provide an example of a $C^2$ metric for which the remainder term is not $o(N^{n/2})$. The proofs rely on the uniform stationary phase estimate and the analysis of the wavefront set. Additionally, we present a uniform stationary phase estimate for oscillatory integrals with a phase function that is piecewise $C^2$ and convex on each subdomain. This estimate is applied to derive uniform $L^p$ bounds for spectral projection operators on compact manifolds with boundaries, as well as uniform estimates for the spectral projection operators of the Laplace operator on a polyhedron. We also show that the remainder term in the Weyl law for a polyhedron is $o(N^{n/2})$ if the metric is piecewise $C^2$, and we provide an example of a $C^2$ polyhedron where the remainder term is not $o(N^{n/2})$. The methodology for the polyhedron case follows the approach used for manifolds with boundaries. This study examines the steady-state solutions of the multiscale rarefied gas flow around a sphere. We introduce a novel iterative approach utilizing the discrete velocity model (DVM) to derive steady-state solutions for the discrete velocity Boltzmann equation (Boltzmann-DVM). This method is validated against the direct simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) technique, which employs the stochastic particle method (Boltzmann-DSMC). The results demonstrate that the proposed iterative method achieves steady-state solutions within dozens of iterations, offering a highly efficient alternative to the computationally intensive DSMC method. Furthermore, the study analyzes the impact of the Knudsen number on the flow field. Finally, we investigate the influence of the initial condition on the convergence of the iterative method. Our findings indicate that the proposed method converges rapidly to the steady-state solution regardless of the initial condition, provided the initial state is not excessively far from the target steady state. Consequently, the proposed method is deemed suitable for investigating the steady-state solutions of rarefied gas flows. Additionally, the method's applicability extends to other rarefied gas flow scenarios, such as those involving a flat plate. We present a statistical mechanical framework for analyzing the stability of 2D Pauli crystals, which are charged particles interacting via a Coulomb-like force and subject to a Pauli exclusion principle. This approach enables the calculation of the phase diagram for these systems. Furthermore, we derive the equation of state for a gas of 2D Pauli particles, demonstrating that it aligns with the equation of state for a gas of 2D bosons when the fugacity is sufficiently low. Finally, we examine the stability of 2D Pauli crystals within the context of the 2D Ising model. Our findings indicate that the phase diagram for 2D Pauli crystals is more intricate than that of the 2D Ising model, exhibiting a richer variety of phases. Additionally, we observe that the Pauli exclusion principle can induce a phase transition in a system of 2D bosons. These results are derived using the transfer matrix method. The transfer matrix for 2D Pauli crystals is formulated as a product of two matrices: one representing the Pauli exclusion principle and the other representing the Coulomb interaction. We show that the transfer matrix for 2D bosons can be expressed as a product of two matrices, one of which is identical to the first matrix in the Pauli crystal formulation. This structural similarity facilitates the derivation of the phase diagram for 2D Pauli crystals. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for the stability of 2D Pauli crystals in the context of the fractional quantum Hall effect. Our analysis suggests that the Pauli exclusion principle plays a crucial role in stabilizing 2D Pauli crystals, a conclusion that is consistent with experimental observations of the fractional quantum Hall effect. We also note that the Pauli exclusion principle can induce a phase transition in a system of 2D bosons, a result that is in agreement with theoretical predictions for the fractional quantum Hall effect. In summary, our work provides a comprehensive statistical mechanical interpretation of 2D Pauli crystals, offering a detailed understanding of their stability and phase behavior. This framework is essential for interpreting experimental data related to the fractional quantum Hall effect. Our findings underscore the significance of the Pauli exclusion principle in stabilizing 2D Pauli crystals, a conclusion that is supported by both theoretical predictions and experimental evidence regarding the fractional quantum Hall effect. Ultimately, our study offers a thorough statistical mechanical analysis of 2D Pauli crystals, providing a robust foundation for interpreting experimental results in the context of the fractional quantum Hall effect.

Steganography involves concealing secret messages within innocuous covertexts. While prior research has focused on embedding data in images, audio, and other media, this study examines text-based steganography. We introduce a method that leverages a language model to embed a secret message into a covertext while ensuring the resulting stegotext remains semantically coherent. Our approach utilizes a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network to generate stegotexts that are both semantically meaningful and capable of carrying hidden information. We evaluate our method's performance across various covertext lengths and secret message sizes, demonstrating that it can successfully hide messages of diverse lengths within text of varying lengths. Furthermore, we show that our stegotexts are difficult to distinguish from the original covertexts. Finally, we validate the effectiveness of our stegotexts by testing their ability to conceal messages within real-world text samples. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/rohitgarg123/Text-Steganography.

Unit commitment (UC) is a critical challenge in power system operations, involving the determination of optimal generation schedules for power plants over a specified horizon. This optimization process must adhere to various operational constraints, such as minimum up/down times, ramping limits, and spinning reserve requirements. However, the computational complexity of UC grows exponentially with the planning horizon, making it difficult to solve within practical timeframes. To address this, this paper introduces a novel approach to UC constraint screening by integrating machine learning. Specifically, we propose a cost model that predicts the cost of violating each constraint. By utilizing these predictions, the method identifies and removes constraints that are unlikely to be violated, thereby reducing the problem's complexity. Numerical experiments demonstrate that this proposed method significantly accelerates the solution of UC problems. Furthermore, the method is highly versatile and can be applied to any UC formulation, regardless of the specific constraints included. Finally, the approach is validated using a real-world dataset from the California Independent System Operator (CAISO). The source code is accessible at https://github.com/kaizhou1999/ML-UC. The pressure-induced evolution of the magnetic structure in the Kitaev material $\alpha$-Li$_2$IrO$_3$ was investigated using neutron diffraction. At ambient pressure, the compound exhibits a long-range antiferromagnetic order characterized by a propagation vector of $(1/2, 1/2, 1/2)$, with Ir moments oriented along the $c$-axis. Upon applying pressure, the magnetic structure undergoes a first-order phase transition at $P_c = 1.6$ GPa, where the propagation vector shifts to $(1/2, 1/2, 0)$. This change signifies a dimerization of the Ir moments along the $c$-axis, resulting in a doubling of the unit cell. Concurrently, the magnetic moment magnitude decreases from 0.7 $\mu_B$ at ambient pressure to 0.5 $\mu_B$ at 1.6 GPa. The observed dimerization is attributed to the collapse of the antiferromagnetic order, which is driven by the pressure-induced reduction of the $t_{2g}$ orbital degeneracy. This study provides the first experimental evidence of the collapse of antiferromagnetic order in $\alpha$-Li$_2$IrO$_3$ and offers insights into the pressure-induced evolution of the electronic structure. Furthermore, the findings suggest that the pressure-induced collapse of antiferromagnetic order in $\alpha$-Li$_2$IrO$_3$ may be a general phenomenon in Kitaev materials. Finally, the results indicate that the pressure-induced collapse of antiferromagnetic order in $\alpha$-Li$_2$IrO$_3$ could be utilized to engineer a dimerized Kitaev state. This state is expected to host Majorana fermions and non-Abelian anyons, which are essential for topological quantum computing. The study also highlights the potential for using pressure as a tool to explore and manipulate the exotic physics of Kitaev materials. Ultimately, this research provides a foundation for future studies on the pressure-induced evolution of the electronic structure in $\alpha$-Li$_2$IrO$_3$ and other Kitaev materials. Additionally, it underscores the potential for pressure-induced phase transitions to be harnessed for the development of novel quantum materials and devices. Synthetic control methods are widely used to estimate causal effects by comparing a treated unit to a weighted combination of untreated units, known as the synthetic control. This paper introduces a proximal causal inference framework to address two key challenges: (i) identifying the causal effect of the intervention, and (ii) estimating and inferring this effect. We demonstrate that the synthetic control is a valid counterfactual for the treated unit if the pre-intervention data follows a specific linear model. Furthermore, we propose a novel estimator that achieves asymptotic normality and valid inference. Finally, we apply this framework to estimate the causal impact of the 1993 Beijing ban on foreign cars on Beijing's air quality. Our results indicate that the ban significantly reduced air pollution, with an estimated effect size of 10.5%. Additionally, we show that the proposed estimator outperforms existing methods in terms of estimation accuracy and statistical inference. The tau lepton is a fundamental particle that decays into a hadron and neutrinos. Identifying these decays is crucial for physics analyses at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), yet they are difficult to detect due to the invisible neutrinos and the complex, multi-particle final states. The network utilizes a novel set of input variables derived from the tau's decay products and the event's missing transverse momentum. The findings are based on a dataset of simulated proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV, with an integrated luminosity of 36 fb$^{-1}$. The Set-Union Knapsack Problem (SUKP) and Budgeted Maximum Coverage Problem (BMCP) are two NP-hard combinatorial optimization challenges. In SUKP, the objective is to select a subset of items with non-overlapping attributes to maximize the count of covered attributes within a given budget. Conversely, BMCP involves choosing a set of resources to maximize the coverage of a target set of elements, subject to budget constraints. This study introduces a novel local search algorithm designed to address both SUKP and BMCP. The method employs a new neighborhood structure that enables the simultaneous evaluation of multiple potential moves, thereby enhancing search efficiency. Additionally, a new acceptance criterion is implemented to facilitate the exploration of diverse regions within the solution space. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms existing methods on both problems. Furthermore, the algorithm exhibits strong performance on large-scale instances, making it a viable option for real-world applications. Finally, the paper includes a comprehensive analysis of the algorithm's performance. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2000/LS-SUKP-BMCP. Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unity. The covering number of $R$, denoted by $\sigma(R)$, is defined as the minimum cardinality of a set of maximal ideals whose union equals the set of non-units of $R$. In this paper, we investigate the covering numbers of specific rings, including commutative rings with identity, commutative rings without identity, and non-commutative rings with identity. We establish upper and lower bounds for $\sigma(R)$ and demonstrate that these bounds are sharp. Furthermore, we examine the covering numbers of polynomial rings, power series rings, and rings of continuous functions. Finally, we explore the relationship between the covering number and the Jacobson radical of $R$. This work extends the findings of A. R. Moghaddamfar and A. R. K. Narayana, who previously studied the covering number for commutative rings with identity. Additionally, we provide a characterization of rings where the covering number is finite. This study examines a nonlocal traffic model featuring general kernels, specifically addressing the singular limit as the kernel's range approaches zero. We demonstrate that the entropy solution to the resulting local model emerges as the limit of the entropy solutions for the nonlocal models. Furthermore, we establish a quantitative estimate regarding the convergence rate. These findings are derived from a novel nonlocal entropy formulation applicable to a broad class of nonlocal conservation laws. The analysis relies on a combination of techniques, including the maximum principle, the doubling of variables method, and the theory of measure-valued solutions. Finally, we provide a numerical example to validate our theoretical results. The primary contributions of this work are threefold: (i) a new nonlocal entropy formulation for general kernels, (ii) a proof of the singular limit for this formulation, and (iii) a quantitative estimate of the convergence rate. These results are anticipated to be valuable for the analysis of other nonlocal conservation laws. Additionally, we offer a comprehensive discussion on the entropy admissibility of the singular limit, a topic that has not been previously addressed in the literature. Finally, Section 7 outlines several open problems for future research. This study introduces a novel algorithm, Variance Reduction based Experience Replay (VRER), designed to enhance the sample efficiency of policy optimization methods. VRER achieves this by minimizing the variance of the gradient estimator for the policy objective function. We demonstrate that the gradient of the policy objective can be decomposed into two components: one with low variance and another with high variance. VRER mitigates the impact of the high-variance component by utilizing a weighted average of the policy gradient and the policy parameter update. We provide theoretical analysis proving that VRER reduces the variance of the gradient estimator for the policy objective. Empirical results on both continuous and discrete control tasks confirm that VRER significantly improves sample efficiency. Furthermore, we show that VRER can be seamlessly integrated with various policy optimization techniques, including TRPO, PPO, and SAC. Finally, we establish that VRER is compatible with off-policy learning, enabling the use of historical data to further boost sample efficiency. We introduce a method for estimating the point spread function (PSF) in coadded images, utilizing a straightforward and efficient approach that relies solely on the PSF of a single input image. This technique is validated through simulations and applied to the Pan-STARRS1 coadded images. The results indicate that the estimated PSF aligns well with the actual PSF, with a maximum relative error of approximately 10%. This finding is supported by both simulations and Pan-STARRS1 data. Finally, we show that the PSF of a coadded image is independent of the number of images included in the coaddition. These findings are valuable for constructing PSF models for coadded images, which are essential for accurately measuring the photometry and positions of point sources. Additionally, this method is applicable to any coadded image, regardless of the PSF characteristics of the individual input images. Stellar activity significantly impacts the interpretation of exoplanet atmospheres, particularly when observing the modulation of planetary signals caused by active regions. This study examines how stellar activity influences the detection of exoplanet atmospheres in both low-resolution and high-resolution transit spectroscopy. We simulated a Jupiter-sized planet orbiting a Sun-like star with a spot coverage of 1% and a spot-to-plage area ratio of 1:10. Our results indicate that low-resolution spectra are highly susceptible to stellar activity, whereas high-resolution spectra are largely unaffected. Consequently, we conclude that high-resolution spectroscopy offers a robust method for mitigating stellar activity in exoplanet atmospheric characterization. Furthermore, we demonstrate that high-resolution data can be utilized to correct low-resolution spectra, thereby enhancing the accuracy of atmospheric retrievals. These findings are especially critical for upcoming missions like the James Webb Space Telescope, which will observe exoplanets in the near-infrared. We also show that high-resolution spectra can be used to correct the low-resolution data collected by the JWST's NIRCam instrument. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for future exoplanet atmospheric studies. We present a concise proof of the existence of constant curvature metrics on punctured Riemann surfaces, utilizing the developing map approach. This proof relies on the uniformization theorem for compact Riemann surfaces and the Gauss-Bonnet formula. Additionally, we provide an alternative demonstration of the uniformization theorem for compact surfaces with boundary, which also establishes the existence of constant curvature metrics on punctured Riemann surfaces. Furthermore, we offer a distinct proof of the uniformization theorem for surfaces with boundary, drawing inspiration from the work of Jost and Yau. Finally, we demonstrate the existence of hyperbolic metrics on punctured Riemann surfaces by applying the Gauss-Bonnet formula to the Gauss curvature of the developing map. These findings collectively offer multiple perspectives on the uniformization theorem for surfaces with boundary and the existence of constant curvature metrics on punctured Riemann surfaces. The primary objective of this paper is to provide a straightforward and accessible proof of the existence of constant curvature metrics on punctured Riemann surfaces. We believe this approach is more intuitive and easier to understand than the original proof by Jost and Yau. The majority of the sample exhibits redshifts between 1.5 and 2.5, and their infrared luminosity correlates with stellar mass, indicating that most are actively forming stars. We introduce a technique for analyzing non-affine expansion in soft materials, utilizing the ratio of the mean-squared displacement (MSD) of individual particles to the MSD of the continuum field they displace. This approach is validated through molecular dynamics simulations of a glass-forming liquid, where the continuum field is derived from the spatial gradient of the displacement field. The method is subsequently applied to a series of experiments on a model colloidal glass, revealing that the non-affine expansion ratio exhibits a distinct minimum at the point where the system transitions from a liquid to a glass. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this ratio can be calculated from the intermediate scattering function, which is accessible via light scattering experiments. Finally, we show that the non-affine expansion ratio correlates with the non-affine parameter, a quantity that has been successfully predicted using mode-coupling theory. These findings indicate that the non-affine expansion ratio serves as a valuable metric for characterizing the non-affine nature of soft materials. The methodology is broadly applicable to soft materials undergoing non-affine deformation, including those subjected to shear or compression. Additionally, the approach is versatile enough to be implemented using various imaging techniques, such as confocal microscopy, or scattering methods like neutron scattering. The study concludes with an analysis of the complexity for specific instances of these hypersequent substructural logics. The primary innovation of this work lies in its cut-elimination proof, which employs a new technique for handling the cut rule. This study examines how electric fields influence the interaction energies of 166 molecular dimers from the S66 benchmark set. Interaction energies were calculated using the CCSD(T)/aug-cc-pVDZ method, with basis set superposition error (BSSE) corrections applied via the counterpoise method. Furthermore, the impact of the electric field on interaction energy is not uniform across all dimers; it varies depending on the specific dimer and the direction of the applied field. Finally, the relationship between the electric field and interaction energy is analyzed through the lens of the electric dipole moment. These findings are crucial for understanding the behavior of molecular dimers in condensed phases and for developing accurate force fields for molecular dynamics simulations. Additionally, the study provides a comprehensive overview of the electric field effects on the S66 dimers, which can serve as a reference for future research. This study introduces a new non-deterministic uncertainty modeling framework for Industry 4.0 scheduling, designed to handle both discrete and continuous random variables. The proposed model is formulated as a two-stage stochastic program with recourse, where the first stage involves strategic decisions and the second stage addresses tactical decisions. To solve this model, a hybrid algorithm combining the L-shaped method with a genetic algorithm is developed. The efficacy of this approach is validated through a case study focused on a real-world production scheduling problem within a food processing facility. The results demonstrate that the hybrid algorithm is highly effective for the proposed model, achieving an average speedup of 10.5 times compared to the standard L-shaped algorithm. Furthermore, the study confirms that the proposed model yields superior solutions relative to existing models. Finally, the paper provides managerial insights derived from the case study, highlighting the significant impact of uncertainty on scheduling outcomes. These findings suggest that the proposed model can serve as a valuable decision support tool for managers in Industry 4.0 environments. This paper introduces a resilience framework for cyber-physical systems (CPS) that integrates control theory with formal methods. We propose a resilience specification grounded in Signal Temporal Logic (STL) and develop a corresponding controller synthesis algorithm. The resilience property is defined by two components: a safety constraint ensuring the system avoids unsafe states, and a recovery constraint mandating that the system returns to a safe state within a specified time following a disturbance. The synthesis process involves two stages: first, designing a nominal controller for the undisturbed system, and second, designing a disturbance controller to handle disturbances. We demonstrate that the disturbance controller can be formulated as a Mixed-Integer Linear Program (MILP) and provide a sufficient condition for the existence of a feasible solution. Finally, we validate the proposed approach through a numerical example. The primary contributions of this work are: 1) an STL-based definition of resilience for CPS, 2) a MILP-based method for designing disturbance controllers, and 3) a sufficient condition for the existence of a feasible disturbance controller. We present a stacking analysis of the 21 cm hydrogen line data from the Green Bank Telescope's High Resolution ALfalfa Legacy Survey (HRALLS) to investigate the characteristics of compact, faint radio sources. By stacking 10,000 sources with a median flux density of 1.5 mJy and a median angular size of 1.5 arcsec, we identified a significant 21 cm hydrogen line emission signal. The resulting stacked spectrum exhibits a Gaussian profile with a full width at half maximum of 10.5 km/s, a peak flux density of 1.2 mJy, and a full width at 10% of the peak of 20.5 km/s. The source distribution displays a double-peaked structure, with the primary peak at 1.5 arcsec and a secondary peak at 10 arcsec. We interpret the 10.5 km/s width as indicative of a rotating disk, suggesting that the majority of these sources are likely galaxies. Furthermore, the double-peaked angular size distribution implies that the sources possess a complex structure, potentially consisting of a central disk surrounded by an extended halo. This study represents the first detection of 21 cm hydrogen line emission from a stack of compact, faint radio sources. Our findings suggest that these sources are likely galaxies, and the observed angular size distribution indicates a complex morphology featuring a central disk and an extended halo. Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) are extensively utilized in information flow security to model systems with internal states that are not directly observable. This paper introduces a novel, more abstract framework for HMMs, termed Abstract HMMs (AHMMs), which are defined as monads on the category of measurable spaces. We demonstrate that AHMMs are equivalent to a specific construction known as the Kleisli category of the distribution monad. Furthermore, we establish that AHMMs can be represented as a colimit of a diagram consisting of a single object and a single morphism. Finally, we apply this abstract model to the quantitative analysis of information flow, proving that AHMMs are capable of representing both noninterference and probabilistic noninterference. Additionally, we show that AHMMs can be employed to analyze information flow within a broader class of systems than traditional HMMs. The paper concludes by outlining several promising directions for future research. We introduce a privacy metric for location traces that remains robust against prior knowledge of the underlying movement patterns. This metric is defined as the minimum Kullback-Leibler divergence between the posterior distribution of a user's location and the corresponding prior distribution, minimized over all possible conditional priors. We demonstrate that this measure is robust, meaning it remains unaffected by priors that are independent of the specific trace. Furthermore, we establish that this metric is equivalent to the minimum divergence from the prior distribution, minimized over all priors. Finally, we apply this metric to evaluate the privacy of two common anonymization techniques: k-anonymization and l-diversity. Our analysis reveals that k-anonymization fails to provide any privacy protection, whereas l-diversity offers a privacy level proportional to the parameter l. Additionally, we show that the proposed metric is equivalent to the l-diversity measure when applied to location traces. These findings are supported by numerical experiments. Resting-state functional connectivity (rs-fc) has become a widely used method for investigating brain function and structure. However, the statistical power of rs-fc analyses is often constrained by the limited number of subjects, which hinders the detection of subtle connectivity changes. This study evaluates the impact of increasing sample sizes on the statistical power of rs-fc analysis. We utilized a large-scale dataset comprising 1,000 subjects from the Human Connectome Project (HCP) to assess the statistical power of rs-fc in identifying group differences in connectivity. Our findings indicate that sample sizes of approximately 100 subjects are necessary to achieve a statistical power of 0.8 for detecting connectivity differences with an effect size of 0.2. Furthermore, we examined the influence of sample size on prediction accuracy using a machine learning approach. We trained a support vector machine (SVM) classifier to distinguish between subjects with and without schizophrenia using rs-fc data. Results demonstrated that a sample size of around 100 subjects is required to reach a prediction accuracy of 0.75. These results suggest that rs-fc analyses should be conducted with a minimum of 100 subjects to ensure adequate statistical power and prediction accuracy. Additionally, we developed a method to estimate statistical power and prediction accuracy for rs-fc analyses, which can be applied to determine the necessary sample size for a specific study. This approach is particularly valuable for planning future rs-fc studies. The code used in this study is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi1992/PowerEstimation. Finally, we provide a Python package, PowerEstimation, to facilitate the estimation of statistical power and prediction accuracy in rs-fc analyses. Beeping networks consist of wireless nodes that can only transmit or receive a single bit per time slot, known as a beep. This paper introduces a randomized distributed algorithm for name resolution in such networks, where each node possesses a unique identifier. The algorithm enables every node to discover the names of all others within a time frame proportional to the logarithm of the network size. This approach is highly energy-efficient, as it relies on a straightforward strategy: nodes randomly select time slots to broadcast their names. The analysis demonstrates that the probability of a node successfully hearing all names is at least $1 - 1/n$, where $n$ represents the total number of nodes. Furthermore, the study examines the algorithm's performance under various network conditions. Finally, the paper explores the relationship between name resolution and other distributed tasks, such as leader election, and presents a method for leader election in beeping networks. The proposed leader election algorithm operates in $O(\log n)$ time with a success probability of at least $1 - 1/n$. Additionally, it is shown that the algorithm's performance is optimal up to constant factors. The paper concludes by discussing potential extensions and open problems. Code-mixing involves combining two or more languages within a single sentence, a phenomenon that is prevalent in multilingual regions. This study examines code-mixing in the Bengali-English context, where code-mixing points are defined as the locations where one language transitions to another. We introduce PESTO, a novel approach that utilizes these code-mixing points to dynamically generate positional embeddings. By integrating these embeddings with relative positional encoding, PESTO effectively captures the sequential structure of code-mixed sentences. Our results demonstrate that PESTO significantly outperforms both standard absolute and relative positional encoding methods. Furthermore, we show that incorporating code-mixing points into the input sequence enhances performance, and we provide an analysis of how PESTO's positional embeddings influence the model's behavior. This study investigates the pressure-dependent isotope effect and critical temperature of the H$_{3}$S hydride superconductor using the Eliashberg theory. By analyzing the pressure-induced evolution of the phonon spectrum and electron-phonon coupling, we demonstrate that the isotope effect coefficient ($\alpha$) decreases as pressure increases. Furthermore, we establish that the maximum critical temperature ($T_c$) of 203 K occurs at 150 GPa, a value that aligns with recent experimental findings. Our results indicate that the Eliashberg theory accurately captures the pressure-induced variations in both the isotope effect and $T_c$ for H$_{3}$S. Additionally, we observe that the isotope effect coefficient is highly sensitive to the electron-phonon coupling strength, which is governed by the van Hove singularity. Finally, we show that the Eliashberg theory successfully reproduces the experimentally observed pressure-induced suppression of the isotope effect in H$_{3}$S. These findings provide valuable insights into the superconducting properties of H$_{3}$S. The source code used for these calculations is available at https://github.com/ChenYi2019/EPW. We demonstrate that the rational function semifield of a tropical curve is finitely generated as a semifield extension of the tropical semifield. This result serves as a tropical counterpart to the theorem stating that the field of rational functions on an algebraic curve is finitely generated as a field extension of the base field. Furthermore, we provide an algorithm to compute a finite generating set for this extension. As a corollary, we establish that the field of rational functions on an algebraic curve is finitely generated as a field extension of the constant field precisely when the curve possesses a finite automorphism group. Additionally, we present an algorithm to determine a finite generating set for this specific field extension. Finally, we offer an example of a tropical curve whose rational function semifield is not finitely generated as a semifield extension of the tropical semifield. This example also illustrates that the field of rational functions on an algebraic curve can be finitely generated as a field extension of the constant field even if the constant field is not algebraically closed. We also provide an example of a tropical curve where the field of rational functions is not finitely generated as a field extension of the constant field, despite the constant field being algebraically closed. These examples are constructed using a specific class of tropical curves defined by their automorphism groups. We prove that for any finite group, there exists a tropical curve with that group as its automorphism group, and we provide an algorithm to compute a finite generating set for the rational function semifield of such a curve. Finally, we show that the field of rational functions on an algebraic curve is finitely generated as a field extension of the constant field if and only if the curve's automorphism group is finite. We also provide an algorithm to compute a finite generating set for the rational function semifield of a tropical curve with a finite automorphism group. This algorithm relies on a characterization of such curves based on their combinatorial structure. We illustrate this characterization with examples of tropical curves having finite automorphism groups. We establish sufficient conditions for a sequence of Q-processes to converge uniformly to the Q-process of the limiting Markov process. These findings are applied to a broad category of Markov processes, including those with countable state spaces and certain diffusion processes. Specifically, we demonstrate that the Q-processes associated with the Wright-Fisher diffusion with selection and the Wright-Fisher diffusion with mutation converge uniformly to the Q-process of the limiting Wright-Fisher diffusion with selection. Furthermore, we show that the Q-processes of the limiting Wright-Fisher diffusion with mutation possess a unique entrance law, whereas the Q-process of the limiting Wright-Fisher diffusion with selection does not. Additionally, we prove that the entrance law of the Q-process for the Wright-Fisher diffusion with selection is not unique when the selection coefficient is non-zero. Finally, we illustrate that the uniform convergence of a sequence of Q-processes to the Q-process of the limiting Markov process does not necessarily hold for the Wright-Fisher diffusion with mutation. This divergence occurs because the Q-process of the limiting Wright-Fisher diffusion with mutation lacks a unique entrance law, a consequence of the existence of multiple quasi-stationary distributions. This phenomenon is also observed in the case of the Wright-Fisher diffusion with selection. In both instances, the non-uniqueness of the entrance law for the Q-process of the limiting Wright-Fisher diffusion arises from the presence of multiple quasi-stationary distributions. Consequently, the uniform convergence of the Q-processes of the sequence of Wright-Fisher diffusions to the Q-process of the limiting Wright-Fisher diffusion with mutation fails to hold. This result is also applicable to the Wright-Fisher diffusion with selection. The Wright-Fisher diffusion with selection is a Markov process that models the evolution of a population's genetic composition over time, where the selection coefficient represents the fitness advantage of one allele over the other. The Wright-Fisher diffusion with mutation is a Markov process that models the evolution of a population's genetic composition over time, where the mutation rate represents the probability of a mutation occurring in a given generation. The Q-process of a Markov process is a Markov process that describes the evolution of a population's genetic composition over time, given that the process has not yet been absorbed. The entrance law of a Q-process is a family of probability measures that describes the distribution of the process at time zero. A quasi-stationary distribution is a probability distribution that is invariant under the evolution of a Markov process, given that the process has not yet been absorbed.

We present a theoretical investigation into the nematic instability within LiFeAs, a material characterized by a tetragonal crystal structure and a superconducting transition temperature of 18 K. Utilizing a tight-binding model, we calculate the nematic susceptibility for the Fe 3d orbitals, incorporating the experimentally determined Fermi surface. Our findings indicate that the nematic susceptibility remains finite at the superconducting transition temperature but does not diverge, suggesting that the nematic instability is absent in LiFeAs. Furthermore, we observe that the nematic susceptibility is highly sensitive to the hole pocket size, which is governed by the Li doping concentration. Consequently, we propose that LiFeAs may exhibit a nematic instability only within a specific doping range. Finally, we demonstrate that the nematic susceptibility can be enhanced by introducing a small amount of disorder. These results offer valuable insights for interpreting experimental data and guide future research efforts. We present a global fit of the Type-II two-Higgs-doublet model (2HDM) utilizing current experimental data alongside projected results from future colliders. Our analysis incorporates constraints from the LHC, LHCb, and flavor factories, along with anticipated measurements of the Higgs boson's couplings from the High-Luminosity LHC (HL-LHC) and the future electron-positron collider FCC-ee. We examine the 2HDM parameter space under both tree-level and loop-level unitarity conditions, as well as perturbativity. Our findings indicate that the HL-LHC and FCC-ee will significantly enhance sensitivity to the Higgs coupling structure, thereby imposing stricter limits on the 2HDM parameter space. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the 2HDM can accommodate a light CP-odd Higgs boson with a mass below 125 GeV, provided that the CP-even Higgs bosons are sufficiently heavy. Finally, we illustrate that the 2HDM can be consistent with a muon g-2 anomaly of $\Delta a_\mu = (25.1 \pm 5.9) \times 10^{-9}$, with the most viable parameter space occurring when the CP-odd Higgs mass is below 125 GeV. Additionally, we show that the 2HDM can explain the recently observed excess in the $B_s \to \mu^+ \mu^-$ decay rate, with the most favorable scenario again involving a light CP-odd Higgs. These results suggest that the HL-LHC and FCC-ee will play a crucial role in determining the nature of the Higgs sector. Finally, we provide a comprehensive discussion of the 2HDM parameter space, including the implications of future collider data. We introduce a new machine learning framework designed to create self-assembling particles and protocols for self-assembly. We present a comprehensive analysis of the asymptotic behavior of minimal spanning acycles for random complexes, with a specific focus on the extreme values of their Betti numbers. Our findings demonstrate that the extremal degrees of these minimal spanning acycles are governed by the extremal degrees of the underlying random complexes. Furthermore, we establish that the minimal spanning acycles of random complexes possess a finite first moment. Finally, we apply these results to investigate the asymptotic properties of persistence diagrams derived from random complexes. Specifically, we prove that the extremal persistence values of minimal spanning acycles are determined by the extremal persistence values of the random complexes themselves. Additionally, we derive the asymptotic behavior of the expected number of persistence intervals for minimal spanning acycles. As a practical application, we utilize these insights to estimate the extremal persistence values of minimal spanning acycles. Finally, we illustrate the utility of our results by analyzing the persistence diagrams of random simplicial complexes generated via the Linial-Meshulam model. In this context, we determine the asymptotic behavior of the expected number of persistence intervals and the extremal persistence values of minimal spanning acycles. Notably, we observe that the extremal persistence values of minimal spanning acycles for the Linial-Meshulam model converge to the extremal persistence values of the random complexes, whereas the expected number of persistence intervals for minimal spanning acycles is significantly lower than that of the random complexes. These results are supported by numerical simulations. The accompanying code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2000/MinimalSpanningAcycles. Vertical Federated Learning (VFL) is a privacy-preserving machine learning framework designed to train models on data distributed across multiple parties. In this setup, parties share only a minimal subset of features with the server, which then aggregates this information to compute the loss function and gradients for each party. While this approach offers significant privacy advantages, it is vulnerable to privacy attacks. This paper introduces a novel VFL architecture that enables parties to jointly train a model without the server's involvement. We demonstrate that this architecture is susceptible to a new type of privacy attack, which we term the "vertical gradient attack." Furthermore, we propose a defense mechanism to mitigate this threat. Our experimental results indicate that the proposed architecture achieves performance comparable to traditional VFL, while the defense strategy effectively reduces the risk of privacy leakage. Finally, we validate the efficacy of our attack and defense methods using real-world datasets. The source code is available at https://github.com/ChenYi2000/VFL-Attack. We investigate the rare decay of $B$ mesons into a proton and a dark antibaryon, which arises from the interaction of a dark photon with a proton. Utilizing QCD light-cone sum rules, we derive the hadronic matrix element for this process. Our findings indicate that the decay width is highly sensitive to the dark antibaryon mass, with the most favorable outcomes occurring at lower masses. Furthermore, we establish constraints on the dark photon parameter space based on the non-observation of this decay. These results demonstrate that $B$ meson decays offer a promising avenue for detecting dark photons at future high-energy $B$-factories. Additionally, we note that the dark antibaryon produced in this decay could be detected through its annihilation with a proton, yielding a mono-energetic photon. This signature would be observable in $B$-meson decays at a $B$-factory, as well as in proton-proton collisions at the LHC and in proton-lead collisions at the LHCb. Consequently, $B$-meson decays provide a unique and complementary method for searching for dark photons. Finally, we discuss the potential for future $B$-factories to probe the dark photon parameter space, extending sensitivity to lower masses and smaller couplings than currently achievable. This paper introduces a new framework for modeling and analyzing attacks on smart cities, which are defined as urban environments where physical, cyber, and social systems are deeply interconnected. We propose a two-player, two-stage game to capture the strategic interactions between attackers and defenders. In the first stage, the attacker selects a target system to compromise, while the defender allocates resources to protect the city's infrastructure. In the second stage, the attacker launches a specific attack on the targeted system, and the defender responds by deploying resources to mitigate damage. We demonstrate that this game possesses a unique pure strategy Nash equilibrium, which we characterize and analyze. Furthermore, we examine the impact of the defender's resource allocation on the attacker's target selection and attack intensity. Finally, we validate our theoretical findings through a case study involving a smart city's power grid. The results indicate that the attacker's target choice and attack intensity are significantly influenced by the defender's resource distribution, and that the attacker's optimal strategy involves targeting the system with the lowest defense capability. These insights can guide defenders in optimizing resource allocation to minimize potential losses. Additionally, we explore the implications of our findings for future research and practical applications. The proposed game-theoretic model offers a valuable tool for understanding the complex dynamics of smart city attacks and can inform the development of more effective defense strategies. Ultimately, this research aims to enhance the security and resilience of smart cities against cyber-physical attacks. This study addresses the challenge of ranking noisy documents for label noise detection, a critical step in semi-supervised learning. We introduce a novel approach that models document ranking as a noisy label classification task. To mitigate the impact of label noise, we propose a bag sampling strategy that groups documents sharing the same noisy labels. This method enables the use of a group-wise loss function, which is more robust to noisy labels than traditional per-instance loss functions. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing methods in ranking noisy labels. Furthermore, we show that our method effectively detects noisy labels in real-world datasets, leading to improved performance in semi-supervised learning applications. The code is accessible at https://github.com/leeyy1992/label-noise-ranking.

The AWAKE experiment at CERN's Super Proton Synchrotron (SPS) aims to investigate beam-induced plasma wakefield acceleration. In this setup, a proton beam is injected into a plasma, generating wakefields that can accelerate electrons to high energies. A proposed method to detect these fields involves observing betatron radiation emitted by the electrons. This study simulates the betatron radiation spectrum and its dependence on various parameters, including the proton bunch charge, the number of protons, and the plasma density. The results indicate that the radiation spectrum is highly sensitive to the proton bunch charge and the number of protons, whereas it shows only a weak dependence on plasma density. Additionally, the study examines the impact of the proton beam's transverse size on the radiation spectrum. Finally, the study evaluates the feasibility of detecting betatron radiation using current X-ray detectors. The findings suggest that while the radiation is detectable, the signal is extremely weak, making it challenging to observe with existing technology. Consequently, further research and development of more sensitive detectors are required to enable the detection of betatron radiation in the AWAKE experiment. This research will be conducted during the upcoming AWAKE Run 2. The study also explores the potential for using betatron radiation as a diagnostic tool to measure plasma density and proton beam parameters. The results demonstrate that the radiation spectrum can serve as a valuable diagnostic for these parameters. However, the study notes that the required precision for such measurements is very high, necessitating further research and development of more accurate diagnostic tools. Ultimately, this study provides a comprehensive analysis of betatron radiation in the AWAKE experiment, offering insights into its potential applications and limitations. This study introduces a series of provably accurate algorithms for learning differentially private decision trees within a distributed environment. We demonstrate that these algorithms achieve $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-differential privacy and establish a lower bound on their expected error. Furthermore, we present a scalable implementation of our distributed private decision tree learning method and evaluate its performance against existing approaches. Our results indicate that the proposed algorithms are both more accurate and more efficient than current state-of-the-art solutions. Chain event graph models are utilized to analyze data from sequential decision-making scenarios. This paper introduces a Bayesian approach for model selection within these graphs, specifically targeting the estimation of the most probable state. The methodology relies on a specific prior distribution for the transition matrix, which is defined by a set of parameters. To facilitate model selection, we derive the marginal likelihood of these parameters. Subsequently, we develop a model selection procedure that identifies the optimal parameter set by maximizing the posterior distribution. These results offer valuable insights for the design and control of autonomous robots. Plants are highly adaptable organisms that thrive in diverse environments, yet their growth is constrained by their inherent biological structures. The results indicate that our method can successfully design plants that achieve superior light absorption compared to those grown in natural conditions. This research holds significant potential for applications in agriculture, horticulture, and the design of bio-inspired systems. Furthermore, it offers a novel perspective on how to manipulate plant morphology to enhance their performance in particular contexts. Finally, we prove that the boundary of a half-disk in the SLE$_\kappa$ process with force $b$ is the conformal welding of two independent quantum disks, where the mass at the origin is $2-\frac{4}{\kappa}$ and the force $b$ acts as a conformal factor. This running induces a temporary, significant enhancement in the curvature perturbation, which subsequently decays. We demonstrate that PBHs can form during this brief window of amplified curvature. Furthermore, we show that the abundance of PBHs can be adjusted by varying the initial conditions of the curaton field. Finally, we establish that PBHs with masses ranging from $10^{-16}$ to $10^{15}$ g can be generated in this scenario. These findings suggest that the curaton mechanism offers a viable pathway for PBH formation. Additionally, we explore the potential for curaton dark matter and its implications for inflationary models. Our results indicate that the curaton can account for dark matter if the PBH mass falls within the range of $10^{-16}$ to $10^{-10}$ g. Finally, we examine the constraints imposed by Big Bang Nucleosynthesis (BBN) and Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) observations on the curaton model. We find that the curaton can constitute dark matter without conflicting with BBN or CMB data, provided the PBH mass is less than $10^{-10}$ g. However, if the PBH mass exceeds $10^{-10}$ g, the curaton cannot serve as dark matter, as it would disrupt BBN and CMB observations. Consequently, the curaton can only explain dark matter when the PBH mass is below $10^{-10}$ g. We present a theoretical investigation into the chiral spin liquid (CSL) phase within the $J_1-J_2$ Heisenberg model on a square lattice, focusing on both amorphous and polycrystalline configurations. In the amorphous setup, we demonstrate that a CSL phase emerges at the $J_1-J_2$ phase boundary, characterized by a finite topological spin gap and a non-zero Chern number. For the polycrystalline configuration, we find that the $J_1-J_2$ phase boundary evolves into a CSL phase when the system is coupled to a magnetic field. Furthermore, we show that the phase diagram of the $J_1-J_2$ model on a square lattice can be mapped onto that of the $J_1-J_2$ model on a honeycomb lattice. Finally, we discuss the potential experimental realization of these findings using cold atoms. Our results indicate that the $J_1-J_2$ model on a square lattice offers a promising platform for realizing a CSL phase. Additionally, we propose that the $J_1-J_2$ model on a honeycomb lattice can be implemented using a combination of optical lattices and a magnetic field. This model exhibits a rich phase diagram, including a CSL phase, a ferromagnetic phase, and a phase featuring a non-zero Hall conductivity. This study introduces a novel conditional generative adversarial network (cGAN) designed to create synthetic portfolio returns that replicate the statistical characteristics of real data. The model is trained using a conditional autoencoder framework, where the input consists of a concatenation of historical returns and a target distribution vector. This vector is derived from the mean, variance, and correlation of a specified number of assets, serving as the condition for the cGAN. The primary objective is to generate synthetic returns that match the statistical properties of the target distribution. We demonstrate that the cGAN successfully replicates the statistical features of the target distribution and show that these synthetic returns can be utilized to train a portfolio allocation model. Furthermore, we illustrate that the trained model achieves superior performance when tested on synthetic data compared to when it is tested on real data. Finally, we provide an example of a portfolio allocation model trained on synthetic data and applied to real-world data. The results indicate that this approach yields a more diversified portfolio, as evidenced by a lower correlation between asset weights. Additionally, the model demonstrates robustness against changes in the underlying data distribution. These findings suggest that the proposed method is effective for portfolio allocation, particularly in scenarios where data is scarce or non-stationary. Social media has become a vital component of daily life for many individuals, yet it remains largely inaccessible to people with disabilities. This study examines the challenges and opportunities surrounding accessible social media content creation. We conducted a survey of 100 users with disabilities to identify their preferred platforms and the specific barriers they encounter. We conclude by proposing a framework for accessible social media content authoring and outlining potential future research directions.
