This study investigates a secure multiuser downlink scenario where a base station (BS) transmits data to multiple users via a reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS). The RIS is designed to enhance the signal strength of the intended users, while a jamming signal is broadcast to the eavesdropper to degrade its reception. The RIS is modeled as a passive component, meaning it does not amplify the signal. Furthermore, the analysis accounts for hardware impairments (HWI) at the BS, RIS, and the eavesdropper. The primary objective is to maximize the system's secrecy rate by jointly optimizing the BS's transmit power, the jamming power, and the RIS's phase shifts. To achieve this, a non-convex optimization problem is formulated and subsequently solved using a successive convex approximation (SCA) algorithm. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed scheme significantly outperforms existing methods. Additionally, the study examines the impact of HWI on the secrecy rate and analyzes the system's behavior under various conditions. Finally, the paper explores the asymptotic behavior of the secrecy rate as the number of RIS elements approaches infinity. The findings indicate that the secrecy rate increases with a higher number of RIS elements, a larger number of users, and a smaller number of eavesdroppers. However, the rate decreases when HWI is present at the RIS or eavesdropper, and it remains unaffected by HWI at the BS. Finally, the asymptotic secrecy rate is observed to be independent of the number of users. These results highlight the substantial potential of RIS technology to improve the security of wireless communication systems. The paper concludes by outlining several promising directions for future research. Specifically, it suggests exploring RIS-assisted secure communication in the presence of HWI, as well as investigating RIS-assisted secure multiuser systems that incorporate other practical constraints, such as energy harvesting capabilities at the RIS. Additionally, the study recommends examining RIS-assisted secure communication under more realistic channel models, including those with spatial correlation and non-line-of-sight (NLOS) conditions. Finally, the authors propose investigating RIS-assisted secure communication in the context of multi-BS networks. These extensions aim to further advance the understanding and application of RIS in secure wireless communications. The authors believe that these research directions will contribute to the development of more robust and secure wireless communication systems. Executive function involves the ability to plan, organize, and regulate one's own behavior. This paper introduces a new approach to modeling executive function within reinforcement learning (RL) by defining it as a contrastive value policy that resamples and relabels perceptions through hindsight summarization. We demonstrate that this contrastive value policy can be trained using a straightforward algorithm. Furthermore, we show that the resulting policy exhibits a form of hindsight optimization, enabling it to learn from past experiences. Finally, we provide empirical evidence indicating that this method can effectively model executive function in a simple gridworld environment. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/leeyy1992/Executive-Function.

Keywords: executive function, contrastive value policy, reinforcement learning, hindsight optimization, hindsight summarization.

Finally, we demonstrate that every principal bundle arising from a locally compact quantum group action on a commutative C*-algebra is locally trivial. This research covers both heavy-ion collisions and proton-proton interactions. The LHC's upcoming Run 3, scheduled to commence in 2022, will feature a significant increase in luminosity, enabling ALICE to explore new physics domains. Furthermore, the experiment is preparing for future accelerator upgrades, including the High-Luminosity LHC (HL-LHC) and the High Energy Heavy Ion Collider (HEI-C). This paper outlines the ALICE detector's current status and its planned upgrades to ensure optimal performance during Run 3 and beyond. The proposed enhancements are designed to maintain the detector's capabilities in the high-luminosity environment of the HL-LHC and to support the study of QGP in the high-energy heavy-ion collisions anticipated from the HEI-C. The discussion covers upgrades to the inner tracking system, the electromagnetic calorimeter, the muon spectrometer, and the forward detectors. Additionally, the paper addresses the necessary improvements to the data acquisition system and computing infrastructure to handle the anticipated data volumes. Finally, the upgrade strategy for the ALICE trigger and offline reconstruction systems is also presented. The overarching goal of these upgrades is to ensure ALICE remains a leading heavy-ion physics experiment, capable of delivering high-quality data for future LHC and HEI-C runs. This will facilitate a deeper understanding of the QGP and its evolution into hadronic matter. The proposed upgrades are expected to be completed by 2025, in time for the start of Run 3. The HEI-C is anticipated to begin operations in the 2030s. The ALICE collaboration is currently developing a comprehensive upgrade plan to address the detector's needs for these future runs. This document serves as a summary of the ALICE detector upgrade proposal. It is intended to be a living document, with updates and additions as the project progresses. The authors welcome any comments or suggestions. The paper is organized as follows: Section 2 provides an overview of the ALICE detector and its performance; Section 3 details the detector upgrades for Run 3 and beyond; Section 4 outlines the upgrade plan for the trigger and offline reconstruction systems; and Section 5 concludes with a summary. We present a method to detect the timelike Unruh effect by utilizing the entanglement between future and past light cones. This approach relies on the geometric phase, known as the Berry phase, which emerges from the interaction of a qubit with the timelike Unruh effect. Specifically, we demonstrate that the phase shift of a qubit's wave function is directly proportional to the entanglement entropy of the vacuum state across the future and past light cones. Furthermore, we show that the phase shift can be measured by observing the interference pattern of a single photon. Finally, we provide a detailed analysis of the phase shift and entanglement entropy within the context of the Schwarzschild black hole. Our findings indicate that the phase shift is non-zero and exhibits a logarithmic divergence as the qubit approaches the event horizon. This behavior aligns with the entanglement entropy of the vacuum state between the future and past light cones, which also diverges logarithmically near the horizon. Additionally, we observe that the phase shift is non-zero for qubits located outside the horizon but vanishes inside it. This result is consistent with the entanglement entropy of the vacuum state, which is zero when the future and past light cones are entirely contained within the black hole. These results offer a new perspective on the entanglement structure of the vacuum state and provide a novel method for detecting the timelike Unruh effect. Moreover, our findings suggest that the phase shift can be used to probe the entanglement structure of the vacuum state in the vicinity of a black hole. This capability may offer new insights into the black hole information paradox and the nature of quantum gravity. Finally, we discuss the potential applications of our results in quantum information theory and quantum computing. Our findings suggest that the phase shift can be utilized to develop new quantum algorithms and protocols for simulating black hole physics and studying quantum gravity. Additionally, the phase shift can be used to create new quantum sensors for measuring gravitational fields and detecting gravitational waves. These applications have the potential to advance our understanding of the universe and enable new technologies for space exploration and communication. In conclusion, our results provide a new method for detecting the timelike Unruh effect and offer new insights into the entanglement structure of the vacuum state. These findings have significant implications for quantum information theory and quantum computing, and they may lead to new technologies for space exploration and communication. Overall, our work represents a significant step forward in our understanding of the fundamental nature of the universe and its connection to quantum mechanics

Event extraction is a critical task within information extraction, yet it remains under-researched due to its inherent complexity. This paper introduces a novel dataset designed for multilingual event extraction, comprising 1,000 English and 1,000 German articles from the Reuters newswire corpus. The dataset features event mentions annotated with their corresponding event types and arguments. Additionally, we present a baseline system utilizing a BERT-based architecture to demonstrate the dataset's utility. Our results indicate that the baseline achieves an F1 score of 60.2% on English data and 58.1% on German data. The dataset is publicly accessible at https://github.com/robin-berndt/MEE. The source code for the baseline system can be found at https://github.com/robin-berndt/MEE-BERT. Furthermore, we provide a detailed analysis of the dataset's characteristics and the performance of the baseline system. We establish a push-forward formula for the universal vector bundle defined on the moduli space of stable bundles with fixed determinant. This result enables us to demonstrate the positivity of characteristic forms for the moduli space of stable bundles with a fixed degree. Furthermore, we apply this formula to derive an explicit expression for the Todd class of the moduli space of stable bundles with fixed determinant. As a consequence, we confirm the positivity of the top Chern class for the universal vector bundle in this context. Additionally, we provide an explicit formula for the Todd class of the moduli space of stable rank 2 bundles with fixed determinant on a curve of genus 2. Finally, we illustrate the formula with specific examples. These findings are applicable to any smooth projective variety. The work relies on the push-forward formula for the universal vector bundle, which was developed by the second author in his PhD thesis. We also present an alternative proof of the push-forward formula for the universal line bundle on the moduli space of stable rank 2 bundles with fixed determinant on a curve of genus 2, utilizing the formula from the PhD thesis. This alternative approach is based on the push-forward formula for the universal line bundle on the moduli space of stable rank 2 bundles with fixed determinant on a curve of genus 2, which is derived from the push-forward formula for the universal line bundle on the moduli space of stable rank 2 bundles with fixed determinant on a curve of genus 3. We present a spectral-timing analysis of the hard state in the black hole binary Cyg X-1, utilizing data from the Rossi X-ray Timing Explorer (RXTE) and the Suzaku satellite. Our findings indicate that the stellar wind from the companion star, which is expected to be highly ionized, does not significantly contribute to the observed X-ray spectrum. This conclusion is supported by the detection of the Fe XXVI Ly$\alpha$ line at 6.97 keV, a feature that would be suppressed if the wind were a major contributor. Furthermore, the Suzaku data reveal a hard X-ray power-law component with a photon index of $\Gamma \sim 1.5$, which is too steep to be attributed to the wind. Consequently, the wind's impact on the X-ray spectrum is negligible, and the observed emission is instead dominated by the black hole's accretion flow. Additionally, we observed a strong correlation between the power spectral density (PSD) of the 0.1--10 Hz band and the photon index of the hard X-ray power-law component, a relationship that aligns with the properties of the accretion flow. These results suggest that the hard X-ray power-law component in the hard state of Cyg X-1 originates from the black hole's accretion flow rather than the stellar wind. Finally, we note that the spectral-timing properties of the hard state in Cyg X-1 are consistent with those of other black hole binaries in the hard state. These findings are crucial for understanding the spectral-timing characteristics of the hard state in black hole binaries. We analyze the resulting outflows, which are driven by the accretion disk and the merger remnant, and compare them to outflows generated by neutrino-driven and magnetically driven mechanisms. Our results indicate that the outflows are primarily powered by the accretion disk, with the remnant's contribution being negligible. Furthermore, we observe that the outflows are highly magnetized, with magnetic energy reaching approximately 10% of the total energy. Finally, we examine the impact of the equation of state on the outflows and discuss the implications of our findings for the kilonova and gravitational wave signals. These results suggest that the accretion disk is the main source of outflows in BNS mergers, and that the outflows are both highly magnetized and neutrino-driven. We present a statistical analysis of tidal features in massive early-type galaxies (ETGs) with stellar masses exceeding $10^{11} M_{\odot}$, utilizing the Hyper Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Program (HSC-SSP). Our study examines the flux fraction of tidal features, defined as the ratio of tidal light to total galaxy light, across a redshift range of $0.1 < z < 0.5$. We identify 1,000 ETGs displaying tidal features, with 60% classified as having strong features. The median flux fraction for these systems is $0.015 \pm 0.002$, and the distribution of flux fractions follows a log-normal pattern. We observe that the flux fraction increases with redshift, suggesting that tidal features are more prevalent in the early universe. Furthermore, we estimate the merger rate for these galaxies by analyzing the flux fraction distribution and comparing it against predictions from the semi-analytic model EAGLE. Our results indicate that the EAGLE model underestimates the observed flux fraction by a factor of 2.5, implying that the merger rate for massive ETGs in the HSC-SSP is approximately 2.5 times higher than the EAGLE model's prediction. This discrepancy suggests that the EAGLE model may be missing a significant population of massive ETGs with tidal features. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for the formation and evolution of massive ETGs. The HSC-SSP dataset offers a valuable resource for investigating the tidal features of massive ETGs and their role in the broader context of galaxy evolution. We conducted a multi-wavelength follow-up of 11 fast radio bursts (FRBs) detected by the CHIME/FRB Observatory, utilizing the Canada-France-Hawaii Telescope (CFHT) and the Gemini North 8.1m telescope. Our analysis of the data yielded no evidence of optical emission, either concurrent with or delayed relative to the radio bursts. These null results establish upper limits on the optical-to-radio energy ratio ($E_{\rm opt}/E_{\rm rad}$) ranging from $10^{-4}$ to $10^{-2}$, contingent on the assumed radio energy. These constraints are comparable to or exceed the most stringent limits previously set by other FRB studies. Furthermore, we analyzed the optical upper limits alongside existing radio and X-ray data for these sources. We found no correlation between the radio-to-X-ray energy ratio and the optical upper limits, nor did we detect any significant optical emission in the radio-selected FRB sample. Consequently, our findings suggest that FRBs do not exhibit a universal optical component. Additionally, we observed that the optical upper limits for the 11 sources are consistent with the optical upper limits of the broader FRB population. This implies that if FRBs possess a common optical emission mechanism, it must be extremely faint, with an average $E_{\rm opt}/E_{\rm rad}$ ratio of less than $10^{-5}$. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for the potential origins of FRBs. Our data indicate that if FRBs originate from magnetars, the optical emission must be highly suppressed, with $E_{\rm opt}/E_{\rm rad} \lesssim 10^{-5}$. Conversely, if the sources are young neutron stars, the optical emission could be more prominent, with $E_{\rm opt}/E_{\rm rad} \lesssim 10^{-3}$. In either scenario, the optical emission is likely not a universal feature of FRBs. These conclusions are supported by the absence of optical emission in the radio-selected FRB sample and the lack of correlation between optical and radio energy ratios. We also note that the optical upper limits for the 11 sources are consistent with the optical upper limits of the FRB population. This suggests that if FRBs have a common optical emission mechanism, it must be very faint, with an average $E_{\rm opt}/E_{\rm rad}$ ratio of less than $10^{-5}$.

Although recent research indicates that large language models (LLMs) can acquire visual capabilities through natural language descriptions, this study demonstrates that LLMs can also be directly plugged into visual controls. We introduce a straightforward framework that enables LLMs to process and generate images, video frames, and audio clips. Our results show that this approach allows LLMs to perform image classification, captioning, and visual question answering with minimal training. Furthermore, we illustrate that LLMs can be utilized to create image editing tools, such as inpainting and style transfer, by accepting natural language instructions. Finally, we present a proof-of-concept application where an LLM serves as a visual agent, executing a series of image editing operations to fulfill user requests. RingCT is a widely adopted method for ensuring privacy in cryptocurrency transactions. However, its current implementation is computationally intensive, making it difficult to scale. This paper introduces a new Delegated RingCT scheme that significantly lowers the computational burden on both senders and receivers. The proposed approach is fully compatible with existing RingCT protocols and can be seamlessly integrated into current cryptocurrencies. We have implemented the scheme in C++ and benchmarked it against the original RingCT protocol. Our results demonstrate that the new scheme is 10 times faster than the original, with a negligible increase in transaction size. Furthermore, we show that the scheme can be extended to support multiple delegations. Finally, we provide a formal security proof for the proposed scheme. This study investigates the hadronic loop mechanism responsible for the decays $\Upsilon(10753)\to\Upsilon(nS)\pi^+\pi^-$, where $n=1,2,3$. Utilizing the effective Lagrangian method, we derive the relevant interaction vertices and subsequently calculate the decay widths. Our findings indicate that the $\Upsilon(10753)\to\Upsilon(nS)\pi^+\pi^-$ processes are primarily driven by the $\pi^+\pi^-$ loop, with the $\Upsilon(10753)$ decaying into $\Upsilon(nS)$ via this loop. Furthermore, we observe that the decay width for $\Upsilon(10753)\to\Upsilon(1S)\pi^+\pi^-$ is significantly larger than that for $\Upsilon(10753)\to\Upsilon(2S)\pi^+\pi^-$, which in turn exceeds the width for $\Upsilon(10753)\to\Upsilon(3S)\pi^+\pi^-$. These results align with experimental data. Additionally, we predict that the branching ratios for these decays are approximately $1.0\times 10^{-4}$, $1.0\times 10^{-5}$, and $1.0\times 10^{-6}$ for $n=1,2,3$, respectively. Finally, we suggest that future experiments should focus on measuring the $\Upsilon(10753)\to\Upsilon(1S)\pi^+\pi^-$ decay to validate our predictions. Our analysis also reveals that the $\Upsilon(10753)$ state is likely a hybrid meson. These conclusions are supported by the observed decay patterns and the calculated decay widths. The results of this work may assist in the identification of the $\Upsilon(10753)$ state. Furthermore, our findings could aid in the search for the $\Upsilon(10753)\to\Upsilon(1S)\pi^+\pi^-$ decay at the BESIII and Belle II experiments. Finally, we recommend that future research explore the $\Upsilon(10753)\to\Upsilon(2S)\pi^+\pi^-$ and $\Upsilon(10753)\to\Upsilon(3S)\pi^+\pi^-$

Distance labeling schemes assign a label to each vertex in a graph such that the distance between any two vertices can be determined solely from their labels. This paper introduces a fault-tolerant distance labeling scheme for planar graphs, where the labels remain valid even after the removal of a single edge. Our scheme utilizes labels of size $O(\log^2 n)$ and achieves a query time of $O(\log n)$. This represents an improvement over the previous best scheme, which had a label size of $O(\log^3 n)$ and a query time of $O(\log^2 n)$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our scheme can be extended to handle the deletion of $k$ edges, maintaining the same asymptotic label and query complexities. Additionally, we prove that for any graph class $\mathcal{G}$, there exists a fault-tolerant distance labeling scheme with a label size of $O(\log^2 n)$ and a query time of $O(\log n)$. Finally, we establish that for every planar graph $G$ with $n$ vertices, there exists a distance labeling scheme with a label size of $O(\log^2 n)$ and a query time of $O(\log n)$. We also show that this bound is tight up to constant factors by presenting a planar graph $G$ with $n$ vertices where any distance labeling scheme requires a label size of $\Omega(\log^2 n)$. We investigate a driven, open optical-lattice system featuring a scar-like mode, which is engineered to remain isolated from the dissipative environment. By applying a Floquet drive to this mode, we induce a transition from a thermal state to a Bose-condensed state. This Floquet-heating mechanism is demonstrated through both analytical and numerical methods. Furthermore, we show that the Floquet drive can be tuned to achieve a non-equilibrium steady state characterized by a non-trivial phase distribution. These findings offer a pathway to engineer novel quantum phases of matter within open systems. Additionally, the proposed Floquet-heating scheme could serve as a valuable tool for quantum simulation and metrology. Finally, we outline potential experimental implementations using ultracold atoms. We introduce a novel stochastic multi-armed bandit framework where the delay in observing an arm's reward is not uniform but instead depends on the specific arm selected. This model encompasses scenarios where delays are either known or unknown. We propose a new algorithm that achieves a constant competitive ratio against the optimal policy when delays are known, and a logarithmic competitive ratio when they are unknown. Furthermore, we establish a lower bound demonstrating that no algorithm can attain a competitive ratio better than logarithmic in the worst case. Finally, we extend this analysis to the nonstochastic setting, proving that our algorithm maintains a logarithmic competitive ratio against the optimal policy even when the arm's delay distribution is an arbitrary, unknown function of the chosen arm. Additionally, we generalize the problem to a setting with multiple experts, where each expert possesses a distinct delay function. In this scenario, we present an algorithm that achieves a logarithmic competitive ratio against the optimal expert. Our findings are supported by a comprehensive set of proofs. This study introduces a novel probabilistic surrogate model for offshore wind turbine loads, utilizing a chained Gaussian process (CGP) framework. The model is constructed by sequentially linking Gaussian process regression models, where each component maps a specific input variable to a corresponding output variable. This approach is particularly advantageous for scenarios where the relationship between input and output data is complex and non-linear. The proposed model is evaluated against a standard Gaussian process regression model and a multi-fidelity Gaussian process model. Results indicate that the chained Gaussian process model achieves superior accuracy compared to the other two methods. Furthermore, the model demonstrates the ability to capture the non-linear dependencies between input and output data, as well as the interdependencies among output variables. Finally, the model is applied to predict the time history of the tower base bending moment for an offshore wind turbine. The analysis reveals that the chained Gaussian process model can accurately represent the non-linear relationship between wind speed and the tower base bending moment, as well as the interdependencies between the tower base bending moment and the blade root bending moment. These findings suggest that the chained Gaussian process model is a promising tool for probabilistic surrogate modeling of offshore wind turbine loads. This study introduces a new method for reconstructing time-resolved data from noisy measurements, with a specific focus on recovering time-dependent diffusion coefficients in reaction-diffusion systems. The approach employs a forward-optimization strategy within a trajectory basis, where the basis functions are derived from the solutions of a linearized system. This linearization is achieved by applying a first-order finite difference scheme to the forward problem, utilizing a time step that is significantly smaller than the one used for data inversion. The resulting method is computationally efficient and demonstrates robustness against noise. Furthermore, the forward-optimization framework is versatile, allowing for the recovery of other time-dependent parameters, such as time-dependent source terms. Numerical experiments confirm the method's accuracy and robustness, and the code is publicly accessible. The authors intend to extend this work to address inverse problems involving time-dependent parameters in nonlinear reaction-diffusion systems. The COVID-19 pandemic has spurred numerous initiatives to curb its spread, with contact tracing being a primary focus. This paper examines the privacy implications of the Coronavírus-SUS application, a contact tracing tool developed by Brazil's Ministry of Health. We demonstrate that the app's architecture and data processing methods fail to adequately safeguard user privacy. Furthermore, we propose a set of recommendations to enhance the app's privacy protections. Our analysis is grounded in the Brazilian General Data Protection Law (LGPD) and the European Union's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). Additionally, we outline a methodology for evaluating the privacy of contact tracing applications, which can be applied to other similar systems. Finally, we discuss the potential impact of our findings on the development of future contact tracing solutions. Quantum information theory offers a framework for describing information processing within physical systems. This review examines the application of this theory to neural systems, focusing on the quantum characteristics of information flow in both classical and quantum neural networks. We explore the potential of quantum information theory to elucidate the information processing mechanisms of neural systems and to enhance the design of artificial neural networks. Furthermore, we outline the challenges and future research directions associated with this field. We present a C code generator for ACL2 that produces proofs of correctness alongside the generated code. This generator is grounded in a shallow embedding of C within ACL2, which is extended to support a broad spectrum of C constructs. The embedding is designed to facilitate the generation of proofs demonstrating that the embedded C code corresponds to its ACL2 representation. The tool is implemented as a library of ACL2 functions and macros, with its core logic encapsulated in a single macro. We have applied this generator to verify the correctness of a C implementation of a simple compiler written in ACL2. Additionally, we have utilized it to generate proofs for various C code examples, including a C program that computes the greatest common divisor of two integers. The tool is accessible at https://github.com/ACL2/ACL2/tree/master/codegen. Our findings indicate that the code generator is highly effective for verifying C code that is straightforward to embed in ACL2. However, we also observed that the proofs produced by the generator are often excessively verbose, suggesting that further research is needed to develop a more efficient proof generation strategy. Signal's end-to-end encryption relies on a 6-digit PIN to safeguard users' privacy. However, the company has not conducted research into how users perceive this PIN, leaving it unclear whether users understand its purpose or how they interact with it. This study investigates user perceptions of the Signal PIN through a survey of 1,000 Signal users. The findings reveal that many users are unaware of the PIN's function, and those who do know it often lack confidence in their ability to set one up. Additionally, users who are aware of the PIN tend to view it as a security measure, yet they frequently fail to recognize the specific risks associated with not using it. These results highlight a significant gap between Signal's design and user understanding, suggesting that the company must prioritize educating its user base about the PIN to ensure effective adoption. The paper concludes by offering design recommendations to improve user comprehension and engagement with the PIN. Furthermore, it explores the broader implications of these insights for the design of other security mechanisms. The study's data and code are accessible at https://github.com/SignalApp/signal-pin-study. The generalized Gauss-Newton (GGN) matrix is a fundamental component in second-order optimization, offering a more robust approximation of the Hessian than the standard Gauss-Newton (GN) matrix. However, the GGN's rank can be prohibitively high, making it difficult to store and computationally expensive to invert. To address this, we introduce ViViT, a low-rank approximation of the GGN that maintains the same rank as the original matrix. ViViT is constructed by combining two low-rank approximations of the GN matrix, which are derived from the Jacobian of the gradient. We demonstrate that ViViT is both accurate and efficient, and we provide a comprehensive analysis of its theoretical properties. Furthermore, we present numerical results that highlight the advantages of ViViT over existing low-rank approximations. Finally, we apply ViViT to the training of deep neural networks, showing that it yields significant speedups compared to the GN matrix. Traffic forecasting is a critical component of intelligent transportation systems, yet it remains difficult due to the inherent sparsity of traffic data. This paper introduces a new approach to address this challenge by leveraging similarity-based feature extraction. The proposed method first identifies similar traffic patterns using a similarity metric, then constructs a feature matrix from these patterns to enhance the forecasting model. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach significantly improves prediction accuracy for large-scale sparse traffic forecasting. Furthermore, the method's effectiveness is validated across multiple real-world datasets. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2019/STF.

We introduce VACA, a variational graph autoencoder designed to handle interventional and counterfactual queries. This model is trained using a new objective function that integrates the likelihood of observed data with the KL-divergence between the true and approximate posterior distributions of latent variables. VACA is capable of generating synthetic data that adheres to the causal structure of the input graph. Furthermore, we demonstrate that VACA can be utilized to estimate the effects of interventions and counterfactuals. Empirical results indicate that VACA outperforms existing methods in both synthetic and real-world datasets. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/robinmiller/vaca. This study examines the impact of pre-released attributes on a film's gross revenue. We introduce a comprehensive, up-to-date dataset containing 10,000 movies, which includes both pre-release and post-release variables. Our analysis reveals that while pre-released attributes are highly predictive of revenue, they account for only a small fraction of the total variance. Furthermore, we observe that the predictive power of these attributes diminishes as the time window for revenue collection shortens. Finally, we demonstrate that the influence of pre-released attributes varies significantly across different genres. This study examines the stabilization of voltage dynamics within power grids, focusing on the impact of frequency control mechanisms. We introduce a novel analytical framework that links the stabilization of voltage dynamics to the stabilization of frequency dynamics. Utilizing this approach, we derive sufficient conditions for stability and analyze the influence of frequency control on voltage dynamics. Furthermore, we demonstrate that frequency control can enhance voltage stability, a finding illustrated through a case study of a power grid. Finally, we outline the limitations of our analysis and propose potential avenues for future research. The primary contribution of this work is the development of a new analytical method for investigating the stabilization of voltage dynamics. This method is applicable to power grids modeled by differential-algebraic equations, where the algebraic component is linear and the differential component is linear or nonlinear. The proposed analysis relies on the spectral properties of the Jacobian matrix of the differential system. Additionally, we establish a sufficient condition for the stabilization of frequency dynamics, which is valid for both linear and nonlinear frequency dynamics. We introduce a model for baryon production during the quantized fragmentation of a QCD string, which incorporates a helical profile and a linearly rising confining potential. This framework is extended to include the creation of baryon-antibaryon pairs. The resulting baryon multiplicity distributions are calculated and compared against experimental data. Furthermore, we derive the corresponding rapidity distributions and compare them with the rapidity gaps observed in the STAR experiment. Finally, we examine the influence of the string's helical profile on the generated baryon multiplicity. The model demonstrates good agreement with experimental data, particularly regarding the rapidity gap distributions. Additionally, we find that the baryon multiplicity is sensitive to the string's helical profile. These findings suggest that the helical profile of the QCD string may play a significant role in baryon production. The model's applicability to heavy-ion collisions is also discussed. We present a new method for calculating the contribution of solar surface flows to helioseismic travel-time measurements. This approach utilizes a surface flow field derived from the Doppler shift of the continuum intensity, which is subsequently smoothed to a depth of 100 km. The resulting travel-time contributions are computed by solving the linearized acoustic wave equation. Our findings indicate that the mean flow within active regions generates a significant travel-time contribution, which is highly sensitive to the flow's strength and spatial distribution. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the observed north-south asymmetry in helioseismic travel times can be partially attributed to the travel-time contributions arising from surface flows. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for the solar dynamo. This study is the first to quantify the impact of surface flows on helioseismic travel-time measurements. The methodology is applicable to any surface flow field, including those of other stars. The code used to compute travel-time contributions is publicly available. This paper introduces a new disparity-aware deep learning framework designed for compressing light field images. The approach integrates a disparity-aware model with a deep learning-based compression architecture. The disparity-aware model leverages the disparity map to enhance the efficiency of the compression model, while the deep learning component utilizes a multi-scale feature extraction network to capture rich features from the disparity map. These features are then fed into a compression model that employs a multi-scale feature fusion network to integrate information from various scales. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art techniques. Furthermore, the method exhibits robustness across different light field images and remains effective even when the disparity map is noisy. Small-area estimation (SAE) is a statistical method used to derive reliable estimates for small geographic units, such as districts or villages, where direct data collection is often too costly or impractical. This study compares two SAE approaches—design-based and model-based—applied to the 2011 census data from Nepal, a low- and middle-income country. Using a dataset of 7,531 villages, we estimated the prevalence of two key indicators: the proportion of households with access to improved drinking water and the proportion of households with access to improved sanitation. Our findings indicate that model-based SAE yields more precise estimates than design-based SAE for both indicators. Furthermore, we observed that model-based SAE is more sensitive to the choice of covariates, particularly when the number of covariates is large. Consequently, we recommend that model-based SAE be utilized in low- and middle-income countries, provided that the number of covariates is carefully selected to ensure model parsimony. Additionally, we propose that model-based SAE be integrated into the standard census framework in these regions. This integration would allow for the estimation of small-area indicators during the census process, thereby reducing the need for costly and time-consuming post-census surveys. Finally, we suggest that future research in this area should prioritize the development of more efficient and robust model-based SAE techniques. The LHCb experiment has observed the rare decay $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ with a statistical significance of $5.1\sigma$. The measured branching fraction is $(7.2 \pm 1.1 \pm 0.6) \times 10^{-8}$, where the first uncertainty is statistical and the second is systematic. This result aligns with Standard Model predictions. Additionally, the differential branching fraction and forward-backward asymmetry were determined across the entire kinematic range. The data show no significant deviation from the Standard Model, with the most notable discrepancy occurring at low $q^2$, which may indicate a potential violation of lepton universality. Furthermore, the angular distribution was analyzed to search for CP violation, yielding no evidence for such effects. The study also provides the first measurement of the $\Sigma^+ \to p e^+ e^-$ branching fraction, finding it to be $(1.0 \pm 0.2 \pm 0.1) \times 10^{-7}$. This value is consistent with the $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ branching fraction, supporting lepton universality. Finally, the ratio of the $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ branching fraction to that of $\Lambda \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ was measured for the first time, with a result of $0.11 \pm 0.02 \pm 0.01$. This measurement is consistent with theoretical predictions and offers a sensitive test of the Standard Model. The analysis utilized 1.0 fb$^{-1}$ of proton-proton collision data collected at center-of-mass energies of 7 and 8 TeV. Atmospheric dispersion is a critical factor in high-resolution spectroscopy, necessitating precise correction to achieve the best possible wavelength calibration. This study presents on-sky measurements of atmospheric dispersion using the HARPS-N spectrograph at the 3.58 m Telescopio Nazionale Galileo. We measured the atmospheric dispersion coefficient (ADC) across 1000 spectral orders spanning 3800–5000 Å, employing a method that relies solely on the observed spectrum and avoids the need for a dispersion correcter. Our results indicate that the ADC varies with zenith distance, with a mean value of 0.00000125 ± 0.00000002 per Å. Furthermore, we analyzed the ADC's dependence on humidity and temperature, comparing these findings with various atmospheric models. We conclude that the ADC is primarily driven by water vapor content, with temperature playing a secondary role. Finally, we recommend a simple model for correcting atmospheric dispersion that is sufficiently accurate for HARPS-N observations. This model is also applicable to other high-resolution spectrographs, such as HARPS, ESPRESSO, and HIRES, provided their ADCs are known. Additionally, we provide a practical method for measuring the ADC using a single spectrum. The data and analysis code are accessible via the HARPS-N website. This paper examines these issues and proposes a novel framework that integrates differential privacy into FL to safeguard user privacy. This study introduces a new framework for an IRS-assisted wireless powered network that incorporates interference. The IRS is strategically positioned to enhance the harvested energy of the wireless power transfer (WPT) system, while the interference source is modeled as a Gaussian random variable. The primary objective is to maximize the network's throughput by jointly optimizing the IRS phase shifts, the power allocation for the WPT system, and the interference power. To achieve this, we propose a deep unsupervised learning approach that utilizes a variational autoencoder (VAE) to learn the underlying data distribution and a deep neural network (DNN) to approximate the optimal solution. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves a throughput performance comparable to the optimal solution. Furthermore, the approach exhibits superior robustness against variations in the interference power distribution and the number of IRS reflecting elements. Finally, the method displays remarkable computational efficiency, with a training time of only 0.001 seconds. These findings indicate that the proposed solution is highly suitable for practical applications. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ahmedmohamed1999/IRS-WPT. This paper introduces a data-driven control framework designed to learn control policies for systems with unknown dynamics, utilizing only a limited number of system trajectories. The proposed method relies on a data-driven controller that integrates a model predictive control (MPC) scheme with a data-driven model of the system dynamics. This data-driven model is trained via a novel algorithm that employs a Gaussian process to estimate the system dynamics, leveraging side information about the system's state space. The resulting MPC-based controller utilizes this data-driven model to generate control inputs that drive the system toward a desired state. The approach is validated through a simulation of a quadcopter navigating a 3D environment. The results demonstrate that the proposed method can effectively learn a control policy for a quadcopter using merely 100 system trajectories. Furthermore, the method successfully enables the quadcopter to perform complex maneuvers, including reaching, swimming, walking, and flying. Finally, the paper provides a theoretical analysis of the proposed approach. The theoretical results establish that the data-driven model converges to the true system dynamics as the number of trajectories increases, and that the control input generated by the MPC-based controller converges to the optimal control input as the number of trajectories grows. These findings indicate that the proposed method is both effective and efficient for learning control policies for systems with unknown dynamics. Finally, the paper will address the method's robustness to model uncertainties and external disturbances. We introduce a twin-field quantum key distribution (TF-QKD) protocol that operates without phase locking. In this scheme, Alice and Bob randomly select between two encoding methods: one utilizing phase modulation and the other employing random bit flips. Open-vocabulary object detection (OVOD) aims to identify novel object categories without requiring specific training data. While current methods typically rely on image-level labels to generate pseudo bounding boxes for training, this approach is often inefficient and prone to errors. To address these limitations, we introduce a new pseudo bounding box generation technique that utilizes both image-level and object-level annotations. This method effectively mitigates the issues of noise and inefficiency inherent in existing approaches. Furthermore, we propose a novel training strategy that leverages the complementary strengths of both annotation types. Extensive experiments on the COCO and PASCAL VOC datasets demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance. The code is available at https://github.com/ChenYiYi/ovod. The [Ne II] emission reveals a compact ionized region with a radius of approximately 0.15", which we attribute to the S1 star. This ionized gas is surrounded by a broader region of atomic hydrogen, roughly 0.5" in radius, which is itself encircled by a larger area of PDR gas extending about 1.5" from the star. We estimate the ionizing photon flux from S1 to be $Q(H^0) \sim 10^{45}$ s$^{-1}$, a value consistent with the star's spectral type of B1.5. The PDR gas exhibits a temperature of $T \sim 1000$ K and a density of $n(H) \sim 10^3$ cm$^{-3}$. We propose that the PDR gas is confined by the atomic hydrogen layer, which acts as a pressure barrier. Furthermore, we suggest that the HI region may be influenced by the nearby S2 star, which is located approximately 0.5" away. This study evaluates the performance of time-varying versus time-invariant factor loadings within factor models used for forecasting mortality rates. We introduce a novel time-varying factor model that employs a time-varying factor loading matrix, where each element is modeled as a first-order autoregressive process. This approach is contrasted with a time-invariant factor model, which utilizes a constant factor loading matrix. The analysis focuses on forecasting the central death rate for the 75+ age group in the United States. Empirical results indicate that the time-varying factor model outperforms the time-invariant version, as well as other established forecasting methods. Furthermore, the time-varying model demonstrates superior accuracy in predicting the timing of the lowest central death rate. Finally, we apply the time-varying factor model to forecast the central death rate for the 65+ age group in the United Kingdom. The findings suggest that the model's effectiveness is not limited to the U.S. population, as it also yields better forecasts for the UK. These outcomes highlight the model's potential utility for forecasting mortality rates across various populations. Additionally, the time-varying factor model offers a more flexible framework for analyzing the dynamics of mortality rates. By decomposing the central death rate into a factor component and a residual component, the model enables the examination of the temporal evolution of the factor loading matrix. This capability facilitates the investigation of how the relative contributions of different factors to the central death rate have shifted over time. Consequently, the time-varying factor model serves as a valuable tool for understanding the dynamics of mortality rates. The paper concludes with a discussion of the model's limitations and potential avenues for future research. Specifically, we propose extending the model to incorporate non-linear dynamics and exploring the application of machine learning techniques to enhance forecasting accuracy. Moreover, the model could be adapted to forecast other demographic indicators, such as fertility and migration rates. Finally, we suggest investigating the model's performance in forecasting mortality rates for developing countries, where data availability and quality may present unique challenges. Overall, the time-varying factor model represents a promising approach for mortality forecasting that warrants further research and development. By addressing its limitations and exploring its applications, researchers can continue to refine the model and expand its utility in demographic forecasting. Ultimately, the time-varying factor model offers a versatile and powerful tool for understanding and predicting mortality trends across diverse populations. However, the high computational costs associated with NAS have hindered its widespread adoption. To address this, researchers have developed various techniques to reduce the search space and accelerate the search process. This paper introduces a novel approach that mitigates interference between different architectures during the search. By leveraging the concept of architecture similarity, we propose a new metric to quantify the interference between two architectures. Furthermore, we introduce a new algorithm that utilizes this metric to identify and eliminate redundant architectures, thereby reducing interference. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art techniques. Additionally, we show that our approach can be integrated with other NAS methods to further enhance performance. We introduce a sum rule for energy deposition eigenchannels in scattering systems, which is derived from the conservation of energy and particle number. This rule indicates that the total energy deposited by all eigenchannels equals the product of the incident energy and the total scattering cross section. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the energy deposition cross section can be expressed as a weighted sum of the eigenchannels, where the weights are determined by the incident wave function. Finally, we apply this sum rule to analyze energy deposition in graphene nanoribbons. Our findings reveal that the energy deposition cross section exhibits a sharp peak at the Dirac point, a phenomenon attributed to the existence of a single eigenchannel with a unit weight at this specific energy. Additionally, we observe that the energy deposition cross section is highly sensitive to the width of the ribbon. These results provide a foundation for understanding energy deposition in scattering systems and may have significant implications for the design of graphene-based electronic and optoelectronic devices. The methodology employed is applicable to a broad range of scattering systems. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are widely recognized for their ability to extract spatially localized features, a capability that has driven their success in image classification. This study investigates whether the superior performance of CNNs stems from their inductive bias or from the presence of a winning lottery ticket (WLT) within their architecture. We introduce a method to identify WLTs in fully connected networks (FCNs) by pruning connections with small weights. Our findings indicate that the WLTs discovered in FCNs are not spatially localized, suggesting that CNNs do not inherently possess a stronger inductive bias for feature extraction. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the WLTs identified in CNNs can be successfully transferred to FCNs, achieving comparable performance. These results imply that the inductive bias of CNNs is not the primary driver of their success in image classification. Instead, we propose that the success of CNNs arises from the fact that their WLTs are more easily discoverable than those in FCNs. This hypothesis is supported by experiments showing that WLTs in CNNs can be found with fewer iterations and less computational cost compared to FCNs. Additionally, we observe that the WLTs in CNNs are more sparse than those in FCNs, which may explain why CNNs are more efficient in terms of both computational resources and time. Finally, we show that the WLTs in CNNs can be further pruned to reduce the number of parameters without significantly compromising performance. These findings offer valuable insights for designing more efficient neural networks. The code is available at https://github.com/zhongyuanwang/Winning-Lottery-Ticket. Our findings indicate that a ticket's expected value is not constant; rather, it rises as the count of future players increases. Consequently, the optimal strategy involves selling tickets to current players while reserving them for sale to those who join later. We derive an explicit formula for the expected value of a ticket and determine the optimal selling strategy, which depends on the specific lottery rules. Furthermore, we examine the impact of ticket resale on the optimal strategy and demonstrate that it can be beneficial to sell tickets to both current and future players. Finally, we apply our framework to the Powerball lottery to illustrate the practical implications of our results. Our analysis reveals that the expected value of a Powerball ticket can vary by up to 10% depending on when it is purchased. Additionally, we find that the optimal strategy for Powerball involves selling tickets to current players and holding them for future players, with the optimal selling price being approximately 1.5 times the ticket's expected value. This pricing strategy ensures that the seller's expected profit is positive. Finally, we show that allowing ticket resale can increase the seller's expected profit by up to 20%. These results suggest that lottery players should consider the timing of their purchases and the potential for resale when making investment decisions. Overall, our framework provides a comprehensive approach to analyzing lottery ticket valuation and decision-making, with broad applications across various lotteries and markets. The valley degree of freedom in two-dimensional materials is a promising candidate for next-generation electronic and spintronic devices. However, electron-phonon coupling can significantly influence valley physics, yet its impact remains poorly understood. This study investigates how various electron-phonon coupling mechanisms affect valley physics in graphene and silicene. We demonstrate that the deformation potential mechanism is the primary driver of electron-phonon interactions, while the piezoelectric mechanism plays a secondary role. Furthermore, we show that the spin-valley coupling induced by electron-phonon interactions is highly sensitive to the specific phonon mode involved. Finally, we establish that the spin-valley coupling strength can be effectively tuned by adjusting the lattice constant. These findings offer valuable insights for the design of valleytronic devices. This paper presents the top-performing solution for the Visual Domain Adaptation Challenge at NeurIPS 2022. The challenge involves training a model to detect 10 object categories using a dataset of 100,000 images from the source domain, COCO-2017, and then evaluating its performance on the target domain, ADE20K. The primary difficulty lies in the substantial domain shift between these two datasets. To address this, we developed a domain adaptation framework that integrates a domain discriminator with a feature extractor, alongside a novel domain-aware contrastive learning strategy. This approach successfully aligns the distributions of both image and text features across the two domains. Our method achieved a mean Average Precision (mAP) of 40.8% on the target domain, securing first place in the challenge. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYiYi/DA-CL. t-SNE is a widely used dimensionality reduction technique that has become a standard tool for visualizing high-dimensional data. However, it relies on Euclidean space and the Gaussian distribution, making it unsuitable for data residing on a sphere. This paper introduces VMF-SNE, a novel method for spherical data embedding. VMF-SNE utilizes the von Mises-Fisher distribution to model data points and pairwise similarities, offering a more appropriate framework for manifold data. We investigate the two-dimensional Fermi polaron using diagrammatic Monte Carlo techniques. By employing a novel diagrammatic expansion for the polaron self-energy, we achieve high-precision results for the polaron energy across a broad spectrum of impurity-bath coupling strengths. Our findings align well with prior numerical and experimental data. Furthermore, we observe that the polaron energy exhibits a logarithmic dependence on the coupling strength at weak interactions, a behavior that matches the predictions of perturbation theory. Additionally, we analyze the polaron wave function and its momentum distribution, revealing that the distribution retains a Fermi-Dirac form even when the polaron is dressed by the surrounding bath. Finally, we demonstrate that the polaron energy can be accurately approximated by a simple formula derived from perturbation theory. This expression is valid for weak coupling and remains reliable up to moderate coupling strengths. We also provide an analytical derivation of this formula. These results offer a valuable reference for future studies on the two-dimensional Fermi polaron. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2019/2D-Fermi-polaron. We introduce a hybrid digital-analog quantum computing framework designed to simulate fermionic systems. This approach leverages the natural evolution of quantum hardware to execute fermionic gates, thereby reducing the count of quantum gates and the associated circuit errors. We demonstrate the simulation of a one-dimensional spin-1/2 Heisenberg model, which is equivalent to the one-dimensional Hubbard model, utilizing a trapped-ion quantum computer. Our results indicate that the hybrid method achieves a 50% reduction in circuit errors compared to a fully digital approach. Furthermore, we show that the hybrid method can accurately simulate the Hubbard model with a 90% success rate, whereas the fully digital method fails to do so. These findings suggest that hybrid quantum computing holds significant promise for the quantum simulation of fermionic systems. We demonstrate that the Hitchin connection on the Teichmüller curve generated by a Veech surface with genus $g \geq 2$ decomposes into a direct sum of connections, each of which is flat. Furthermore, we establish that the curvature of this connection is proportional to the wedge product of the flat connections. As a consequence, we derive an explicit formula for the holonomy of the Hitchin connection along geodesics within the Teichmüller curve. Additionally, we provide a criterion for the vanishing of the Hitchin connection's curvature, which applies to all known examples of Teichmüller curves. Finally, we prove that the Hitchin connection is flat for the Teichmüller curves associated with the regular octagon and the regular dodecagon. These findings extend the work of Eskin, Rabinowitz, and Zemov, who previously established the flatness of the Hitchin connection for the regular octagon. Our approach relies on the theory of automorphic forms and the geometry of the moduli space of abelian differentials. The ALICE Collaboration presents a measurement of the elliptic flow ($v_2$) of electrons originating from beauty-hadron decays in Pb-Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}$ = 5.02 TeV. This analysis utilizes the ALICE detector's electron identification capabilities, which are optimized for the 2015 data-taking run. The study examines the $v_2$ of electrons in the transverse momentum range 2 < $p_{\rm T}$ < 10 GeV/$c$ across centralities from 0–10% to 50–70%. The observed $v_2$ values are compared with theoretical predictions derived from a hybrid model that combines hydrodynamic evolution with a hadronic cascade. The results indicate that the measured $v_2$ is consistent with the $v_2$ of beauty quarks generated within the quark-gluon plasma. Furthermore, the $v_2$ of beauty quarks exhibits a dependence on centrality and $p_{\rm T}$ that aligns with hydrodynamic model predictions. These findings suggest that beauty quarks participate in the collective flow of the quark-gluon plasma and are rapidly thermalized. Additionally, the study reports the first measurement of the $v_2$ of electrons from beauty-hadron decays in the $p_{\rm T}$ range 10 < $p_{\rm T}$ < 20 GeV/$c$, which is also consistent with hybrid model expectations. Finally, the $v_2$ of electrons from beauty-hadron decays is compared with that of light hadrons, revealing that the $v_2$ of beauty quarks is smaller than that of light quarks at low $p_{\rm T}$ but becomes comparable at high $p_{\rm T}$. These observations are interpreted as evidence for the formation of a quark-gluon plasma and the rapid thermalization of beauty quarks. The results are published in Phys. Lett. B 796 (2019) 134830. We present a method for estimating the persistent homology of chromatic alpha complexes, which are geometric structures derived from a vertex-colored point cloud. This approach is applicable to any chromatic alpha complex, including those formed by the union of individual chromatic complexes. Our technique relies on a chromatic Delaunay triangulation, which we demonstrate can be computed in linear time. Furthermore, we establish that the persistent homology of the resulting chromatic alpha complex is isomorphic to that of the chromatic Delaunay triangulation. We validate this methodology by analyzing the persistent homology of a chromatic point cloud representing a 3D model of a human face. Additionally, we provide a Python implementation of our algorithm, which is available on GitHub. This implementation is designed to be easily extensible for future research. Finally, we outline several potential applications of chromatic alpha complexes in data analysis. Specifically, we show that the persistent homology of a chromatic point cloud can be utilized to identify the number of distinct colors within the cloud. This capability is particularly valuable for color segmentation tasks, where the goal is to partition a colored image into multiple regions, each corresponding to a unique color. In this context, the chromatic point cloud is generated by sampling the image, and the count of distinct colors in its persistent homology serves as a metric for the segmentation's quality. We also demonstrate that the persistent homology of a chromatic point cloud can reveal the number of connected components in the image. Finally, we illustrate how the persistent homology of a chromatic point cloud can be used to determine the number of holes in a colored image. This study examines the gain of optimal power control over binary power control in a $K$-user interference network, where each user's transmit power is either 0 or $P$. We demonstrate that the maximum gain achievable by optimal power control is $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$. This finding contrasts with the $\Theta(K)$ gain observed in the two-user case and highlights the significant difference between the two-user scenario and general $K$-user networks. Furthermore, we establish that this gain is attained in a specific network topology, thereby proving that optimal power control can yield a substantial improvement over binary power control in certain settings. Finally, we extend these results to the Gaussian setting, where the channel matrix is drawn from a Gaussian distribution. In this context, we show that the gain of optimal power control over binary power control is also $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$. This result is notable because it indicates that the gain is not merely a consequence of the network topology but is instead driven by the network's density. Additionally, we observe that the gain of optimal power control over random power control is also $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$. These findings are derived using a combination of information-theoretic techniques and probabilistic arguments. The paper concludes with a discussion of open problems.

Keywords: Interference networks, power control, GDoF, binary power control, optimal power control, random power control.

The stitching algorithm, introduced by M\"{u}ller and Stoyan in 1993, is a straightforward method for generating realizations of the Strauss process, a type of repulsive point process. This paper presents a simulation study comparing the stitching algorithm with two other methods: the rejection algorithm and the Gibbs sampler. Results indicate that the stitching algorithm is the most efficient, followed by the rejection algorithm, with the Gibbs sampler being the least efficient. We introduce a scheduling framework for multitasking applications where multiple tasks within an application share a single processor. This model is particularly relevant for multitasking operating systems, as it allows the system to allocate a fraction of a processor to each task, enabling the execution of several tasks concurrently on a single machine. We demonstrate that, under specific conditions, the optimal schedule can be determined in polynomial time. Furthermore, we establish that the problem becomes strongly NP-hard when the number of tasks is fixed at three or more, and NP-hard when the number of tasks is exactly two. Finally, we present a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme for the case involving two tasks. Additionally, we prove that the problem is APX-hard when the number of tasks is fixed at three or more. In this scenario, we also provide a polynomial-time approximation scheme for instances where the number of processors is fixed. Finally, we show that the problem is strongly NP-hard even when the number of tasks is fixed at two, provided that the number of processors is fixed at two or more. The Internet of Things (IoT) is rapidly expanding, with billions of devices anticipated by 2025. These devices are increasingly deployed in remote, harsh, and unmanaged settings, such as industrial plants, where they must operate reliably for years. A critical component of this infrastructure is the firmware, which is typically delivered via a central server to the IoT devices. However, this traditional architecture is vulnerable to single points of failure and security breaches. To address these issues, a more resilient and secure approach involves distributing the firmware across a mesh network of IoT devices. This paper presents a performance analysis of such a system, specifically focusing on a large-scale IoT network utilizing the LoRaWAN protocol. We evaluate the system's performance under various conditions, including different numbers of devices, varying packet loss rates, and diverse network topologies. Our findings indicate that a mesh network can successfully deliver firmware to all devices in a large-scale IoT environment, even when accounting for packet loss. Furthermore, we observe that the system's performance is highly sensitive to the specific topology of the mesh network. Universal adversarial examples are inputs that cause a classifier to produce incorrect outputs across all models within a specific family. This study examines the creation of universal adversarial perturbations for quantum classifiers. We demonstrate that for a broad category of quantum classifiers, a single perturbation exists that is universally effective. Furthermore, we establish that for any quantum classifier, a single perturbation can be generated that remains effective against all other quantum classifiers. Finally, we present a method to construct a perturbation that is effective against all quantum classifiers of a given size. These findings are derived from a comprehensive analysis of the mathematical properties of quantum classifiers. Additionally, we provide numerical evidence supporting the existence of universal adversarial perturbations for quantum classifiers. Our results indicate that the probability of a quantum classifier outputting a correct result can be significantly reduced by a single perturbation, even when the perturbation is applied to only a small fraction of the input qubits. This suggests that quantum classifiers may be highly vulnerable to adversarial attacks. These insights could guide the development of more robust quantum classifiers and offer a foundation for future research into adversarial attacks on quantum machine learning models. This paper investigates Steklov eigenvalues for nearly spherical domains. Conformance checking is a core component of process mining, designed to identify discrepancies between actual process executions and the modeled process flow. While existing methods typically analyze complete event logs, this paper introduces infix and postfix alignments to handle partial event data. These alignments are specifically tailored for scenarios where event logs contain missing data, such as when only specific process fragments are recorded. Power system expansion planning (PSEP) models are essential for determining the optimal generation and transmission infrastructure to meet future demand. However, these models rely on numerous assumptions, and their outcomes are highly sensitive to variations in input parameters. This study examines how input uncertainties influence the results of a PSEP model applied to the Nordic power system. We analyze the impact of uncertainty in future electricity demand, generation costs, and transmission capacity limits. Our findings indicate that while demand uncertainty has a negligible effect on the optimal solution, variations in generation costs and transmission capacity constraints significantly alter the results. Consequently, we propose a method to quantify the sensitivity of PSEP model outcomes to input uncertainties. This approach involves solving the model multiple times with varied input parameters and calculating the resulting differences in the optimal solution. We demonstrate the application of this methodology using the Nordic power system. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for PSEP models and their application in practice. We introduce a rheo-acoustic setup designed to generate and control ultrasonic standing waves within a colloidal suspension. This device enables the creation of a colloidal gel by inducing particle aggregation at the acoustic pressure antinodes. By adjusting the ultrasonic frequency and amplitude, we can precisely regulate the gel's mechanical characteristics, including its yield stress and elastic modulus. Furthermore, we demonstrate that applying a shear force to the gel results in a non-Newtonian fluid with a tunable viscosity. We present a comprehensive analysis of non-resonant diagrams contributing to the single production of top and bottom partners at the LHC. These contributions are significant in scenarios where the partner masses are comparable to the electroweak scale, a condition that also enhances the associated production of the partner with a Higgs boson. Our findings indicate that the non-resonant diagrams can yield cross sections comparable to those of the Higgs-mediated processes. Furthermore, we examine the impact of these non-resonant diagrams on the kinematic distributions of the final states. We observe that these diagrams can substantially alter the distributions, particularly in the tails, thereby affecting the sensitivity of various kinematic variables used in experimental searches. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for current and future experimental searches. Our analysis demonstrates that the non-resonant diagrams can significantly affect the sensitivity of existing searches, and we provide recommendations for future experimental efforts. We conclude that it is essential to include these non-resonant diagrams in the analysis of single production of top and bottom partners at the LHC. Neural Machine Translation (NMT) has become a primary method for creating query translators, which convert queries from one knowledge base to another. However, these systems often fail to capture the full meaning of source queries, leading to incomplete translations. This paper introduces a copy mechanism designed to address this issue by directly copying elements from the input query into the output. We evaluate the approach using a neural machine translation model based on the attention mechanism. Experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms the baseline, achieving a 10% increase in query coverage. Additionally, we analyze the model's behavior to provide insights into its operation. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/robin-lee/SPARQL-NMT. This study examines the thermodynamic characteristics of monolayer graphene under an electric field, focusing on its specific heat, compressibility, and thermal expansion coefficient. Additionally, the research explores the potential for detecting the Dirac point through thermal expansion measurements. Finally, the study examines the impact of the electric field on the thermal expansion coefficient, demonstrating that it can be tuned to achieve values as high as $10^{-2}$. This suggests that the thermal expansion coefficient of graphene can be effectively controlled by adjusting the electric field. Overall, these findings highlight the potential for utilizing thermal expansion as a tool for characterizing graphene. The research underscores the unique thermodynamic properties of graphene and its suitability for applications in thermal management and sensing. This study identified 11 radio bursts, with the majority detected by LOFAR. The bursts exhibit a wide range of durations, from 10 to 1000 seconds, and display a power-law distribution of peak flux densities with a slope of $\alpha = 1.7$. The observed radio emission is attributed to the electron-cyclotron maser instability, driven by the star's strong magnetic field. Furthermore, the bursts are linked to stellar flares, as evidenced by their temporal correlation with optical flares. The radio bursts exhibit a power-law distribution in peak flux density with a slope of $\alpha = 1.8$, a finding consistent with other flare stars. Additionally, we observed a correlation between the peak flux density and the duration of the bursts, which can be explained by the varying distances of the emission sources from the star. We present findings from a cluster quantum Monte Carlo investigation into the thermodynamic characteristics of two-dimensional frustrated trimer antiferromagnets. This study introduces a new kinetic model featuring a velocity-dependent collision frequency, designed to capture the impact of intermolecular potential on rarefied gas flows. The model's collision frequency is derived from the inverse of the mean free path, which is calculated using the Lennard-Jones potential and the Boltzmann collision integral. The resulting kinetic equation is solved via the discrete velocity method, and its performance is evaluated against the constant collision frequency model and the Boltzmann equation. Numerical results indicate that the proposed model effectively reproduces the influence of intermolecular potential on rarefied gas flows. Furthermore, the model demonstrates robustness across a wide range of Knudsen numbers and remains applicable to both simple and complex flow scenarios. Finally, the model is validated by comparing its predictions for the drag coefficient of a sphere with existing literature. These findings suggest that the model holds significant potential for simulating rarefied gas flows in practical engineering applications. Additionally, the methodology employed to derive the velocity-dependent collision frequency can be extended to other intermolecular potentials. Consequently, this work offers a valuable tool for investigating the effects of intermolecular potential on rarefied gas flows. We present spectropolarimetric observations of the A-type star HD 58260, revealing a radial magnetic field gradient. This gradient was detected through spectropolarimetry of NLTE lines in emission, specifically the Ca II H&K lines, which are highly sensitive to magnetic field variations in the stellar atmosphere. The observed data indicate a radial field gradient of approximately 1.5 kG per stellar radius. This finding aligns with the hypothesis that the star's magnetic field is generated by a dynamo operating in its outer convective envelope. Furthermore, the results suggest that the magnetic field strength in the outer convective envelope is roughly 100 times greater than that in the radiative interior. This study represents the first direct detection of a magnetic field gradient in an A-type star. Additionally, we provide a detailed analysis of the magnetic field structure of HD 58260, including its geometry, strength, and evolution. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for the dynamo theory of A-type stars. The data are accessible via the CDS archive. This study introduces a nonparametric approach for estimating conditional expectation operators within reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHS). Furthermore, the method is applied to analyze the relationship between two random variables, with numerical experiments demonstrating its effectiveness. The results indicate that the approach performs well even when the underlying distribution is unknown. Additionally, the method is utilized to estimate the mean function of a stochastic process conditioned on another process. The application yields promising outcomes, successfully capturing the correlation between the two price series. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/robertkroger/condexp. Temporal knowledge graphs (TKGs) are increasingly utilized to model dynamic real-world events, yet their inherent complexity and sparsity pose significant challenges for link prediction. While recent studies have attempted to address these issues by incorporating temporal information, they often fail to fully leverage it. This paper introduces a novel approach that integrates both temporal and non-temporal data into a unified framework. Specifically, we propose a new TKG link prediction model that combines a temporal graph neural network with a static knowledge graph embedding model. Our method employs a multi-head attention mechanism to aggregate node features from neighboring time steps, thereby capturing temporal dependencies. Furthermore, we utilize a multi-task learning strategy to enhance the model's performance. Extensive experiments on two real-world datasets demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the model's effectiveness and interpretability. The source code is available at https://github.com/ChenYi2000/TEKGE.
